m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Install Python 3 (3.10 or newer) from python.org, or from Linux on a Chromebook.
  • Install Visual Studio Code and Microsoft's Python extension.
  • Check the setup from VS Code's built-in terminal with one command.
  • Fix the four problems that stop most people on day one.

The projects in this course are bigger than one file. The quiz game in Module 4 has a program, a file of questions, and a file of saved scores, and you'll want to see all three at once. IDLE, the editor many people start with, opens one window per file and has no built-in terminal. Visual Studio Code (VS Code) shows your whole project folder in a sidebar, runs programs in a terminal at the bottom of the window, and underlines many mistakes before you even run the code.

Everything here is free. Budget about 30 minutes, most of it waiting for downloads.

#Three pieces, three jobs

It helps to know what each piece does, because most setup problems come from one piece not being able to find another.

  • Python is the interpreter: the program that reads your .py file and carries out each line. VS Code does not include it, so you install it separately.
  • VS Code is the editor: where you type, save, and organize files. On its own it knows nothing special about Python.
  • The Python extension (made by Microsoft) is the bridge. It finds the Python installed on your computer, adds a Run button, and powers autocomplete and error underlines.

If you already installed Python 3.10 or newer for an earlier course, skip Step 1 and keep the Python you have.

#Step 1: Install Python 3

Windows

  1. Open python.org/downloads (opens in a new tab) and click the yellow Download Python button.
  2. Open the downloaded file and choose Install. Recent versions of Python for Windows use the Python install manager, which adds the python and py commands.
  3. The first time you run Python, a console window may ask questions, such as whether to install the latest version or add a folder to your PATH. Type y and press Enter for each one.
  4. If you see the older-style installer instead (a window with an Install Now button), tick Add python.exe to PATH at the bottom before clicking Install Now.

macOS

  1. Open python.org/downloads (opens in a new tab) and click Download Python. You get a .pkg installer.
  2. Open it and click through Continue, Agree, and Install. Your Mac asks for your login password.
  3. When it finishes, a Finder window shows a new Python 3 folder in Applications. You can close it; VS Code will find Python on its own.
  4. On a Mac the command is python3, not python. Remember that for the check below.

Chromebook

  1. Open Settings, search for Linux, and turn on the Linux development environment. Accept the suggested disk size. A black Terminal window opens when it is ready.
  2. Linux already includes Python 3. Add the two extra pieces this course needs (virtual environments and pip) by typing:
  1. Check the version with python3 --version. Anything from 3.10 up works for this course.

#Step 2: Install VS Code

Windows

  1. Go to code.visualstudio.com/download (opens in a new tab) and download the User Installer for Windows. It installs just for your account, so it does not need an administrator password.
  2. Run it and accept the license.
  3. On the Select Additional Tasks page, leave Add to PATH ticked. Then click Install and Finish.

macOS

  1. Go to code.visualstudio.com/download (opens in a new tab) and click the Mac download.
  2. Open the downloaded file and drag Visual Studio Code into your Applications folder. Running it straight from Downloads causes odd update problems later.
  3. Open it from Applications. If macOS asks whether you are sure you want to open an app downloaded from the internet, click Open.

Chromebook

  1. In the Linux Terminal, run dpkg --print-architecture. If it prints amd64, you need the x64 .deb download; if it prints arm64, you need the ARM64 .deb.
  2. Download that .deb file from code.visualstudio.com/download (opens in a new tab).
  3. Open the Files app, find the file in Downloads, and double-click it. Choose Install and wait a minute or two.
  4. VS Code now appears in your app launcher inside the Linux apps folder.

#Step 3: Add the Python extension

  1. Open VS Code. Click the Extensions icon in the left bar (four small squares), or press Ctrl+Shift+X (Cmd+Shift+X on a Mac).
  2. Type Python in the search box.
  3. Pick the one named Python whose publisher is Microsoft, with a blue check mark, and click Install.

It brings three helpers along with it: Pylance (autocomplete and error underlines), Python Debugger, and Python Environments (which manages the virtual environments you will meet in the next lesson). You don't need to install those by hand.

⚠️ Watch out

The Marketplace has many lookalikes with names such as "Python Extension Pack" or "Python for VSCode". Some are abandoned and a few clash with the real one. Check that the publisher says Microsoft before clicking Install.

#Check it from VS Code's terminal

VS Code has a terminal built into the bottom of the window. Open it from the menu bar with Terminal → New Terminal, or press Ctrl+` (the backtick key, usually above Tab). Then type the command for your system and press Enter.

Windows

macOS

Chromebook

Your numbers will differ. What matters is that the answer starts with Python 3. and the second number is 10 or higher. If you got that, all three pieces can see each other and you are ready for the next lesson.

#When the check fails

python : The term 'python' is not recognized... on Windows. This almost always means VS Code was already open when you installed Python. A terminal copies the list of program locations (the PATH) when VS Code starts, so it can't see anything installed afterwards. Quit VS Code completely and open it again. If it still fails, try py --version; the py command often works when python doesn't.

Typing python opens the Microsoft Store on Windows. Windows has shortcut "aliases" that point python at the Store. Search the Start menu for Manage app execution aliases and make sure the entries for the Python you installed are turned on, then restart VS Code.

zsh: command not found: python on a Mac. Nothing is broken. macOS only names the command python3. Inside a virtual environment, which you'll make next lesson, plain python works too.

No Linux option in a Chromebook's Settings. School and family accounts often turn it off. Ask whoever manages the device, or use another computer for this course. You can't install VS Code on a Chromebook without Linux.

💡 Tip

When something fails, copy the exact error text before you change anything. "It doesn't work" is impossible to search; The term 'python' is not recognized takes ten seconds.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Open a folder in VS Code and create a .py file in it.
  • Run a file two ways: the Run Python File button and a typed terminal command.
  • Read the command VS Code types for you, and know which Python it used.
  • Create a .venv virtual environment and confirm you're inside it.

When you press Run in VS Code, it does something sneaky: it types a command into the terminal for you, then presses Enter. That one line of text tells you exactly which copy of Python ran your code. By the end of this page you'll be able to read it, type it yourself, and switch the project onto a Python that belongs only to it.

#Step 1: Make a project folder and open it

Every program in this course will live in one folder. Make it now:

  1. In File Explorer (Windows), Finder (Mac), or Files (Chromebook, inside Linux files), create a folder called python-projects. Use lowercase and a dash, no spaces; spaces in folder names cause small headaches when you type paths in a terminal.
  2. In VS Code, choose File → Open Folder… and pick python-projects.
  3. VS Code asks whether you trust the authors of the files in this folder. It's your own empty folder, so choose Yes, I trust the authors.

The left sidebar (the Explorer) now shows PYTHON-PROJECTS with nothing under it. Opening the folder, not a single file, is what lets VS Code treat it as one project.

#Step 2: Write and run hello.py

Hover over the folder name in the Explorer and click the New File icon, then type hello.py and press Enter. VS Code sees the .py ending and switches on the Python extension. Type this in:

Now click the triangle Run Python File button in the top-right corner of the editor. A terminal panel slides up from the bottom, and you'll see a line like this appear before the output:

That's the command VS Code typed. It has two parts: the full path to a Python interpreter, then the full path to your file. On Windows it starts with & and the interpreter path ends in python.exe, but the shape is the same. Look at the first path whenever you wonder "which Python ran this?"

#Step 3: Run it yourself from the terminal

You can type that command in a shorter form. Click inside the terminal and run:

Windows

macOS or Chromebook

You get the same four lines. This works because the terminal starts inside your project folder, so the short name hello.py is enough. That detail comes back in Module 4, when your programs open data files by name.

⚠️ Watch out

The terminal runs the file as saved on disk. If the editor tab shows a dot instead of an ×, you have unsaved changes, and python hello.py will run the old version. Press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac) first, or turn on File → Auto Save so you never have to think about it.

Programs that ask for input work the same way. Click in the terminal when the question appears, type your answer, and press Enter:

#Step 4: Give the project its own Python

Here's the problem a virtual environment solves. In Module 5 you'll install extra libraries with a tool called pip. Suppose one project needs version 1 of a library and another needs version 2. If both install into the same Python, one of them breaks.

A virtual environment is a folder, by convention called .venv, inside your project. It holds a small Python that points back to the one you installed, plus its own private shelf for libraries. Anything you install while it's active lands on that shelf and nowhere else. Delete the folder and the environment is gone, with nothing else on your computer touched.

The easiest way to make one is from VS Code:

  1. Open the Command Palette with Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on a Mac).
  2. Type Python: Create Environment and choose it.
  3. Follow the prompts: choose Venv as the type, then choose the Python you installed in the last lesson. If it asks for a name, keep .venv.

After a few seconds a .venv folder appears in the Explorer, and VS Code selects it for this project. If you prefer typing, this does the same job:

Windows

macOS or Chromebook

The first line builds the folder. The second line activates it for this terminal only. VS Code does that step for you in every new terminal once .venv is selected, so you'll rarely type it.

#Step 5: Prove which Python is running

Close the terminal (the trash-can icon on its toolbar) and open a fresh one with Terminal → New Terminal. The prompt should now begin with (.venv). Ask Python where it lives:

The path ends inside .venv, so this is the project's own Python. (On Windows it ends in .venv\Scripts\python.exe.) Notice that plain python works here even on a Mac: an active environment always provides it.

For one more check, save this as check_setup.py and press Run:

The output on this page comes from our lesson server, which doesn't use a virtual environment, so its last line says False. On your computer, with .venv selected, it should say True. The trick is in sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix: inside an environment, Python's own folder (prefix) differs from the folder of the Python it was made from (base_prefix).

#If it went wrong

Activate.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system (Windows). PowerShell blocks scripts by default. Run this once, then try again:

The virtual environment was not created successfully because ensurepip is not available (Chromebook). The python3-venv package is missing. Run sudo apt install -y python3-venv, delete the half-made .venv folder, and create it again.

The prompt has no (.venv), or check_setup.py says False on your computer. VS Code is using a different Python. Open the Command Palette, run Python: Select Interpreter, and pick the entry whose path contains .venv. Then open a new terminal.

💡 Tip

Never save your own files inside .venv, and never copy it to another computer. Environments contain paths specific to one machine. To move a project, copy your .py files and build a fresh .venv on the other side.

#The same idea from another teacher

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You edit hello.py, don't save it, and type python hello.py in the terminal. What runs?

  • The terminal can't see the editor's unsaved text; it reads the file from disk.

  • python opens the file on disk, so unsaved edits are ignored. Save first or turn on Auto Save.

  • Python has no idea the editor has unsaved changes. It just runs what's on disk.

Show answer

B. python opens the file on disk, so unsaved edits are ignored. Save first or turn on Auto Save.

2Your terminal prompt starts with (.venv). What does that tell you?

  • Your code lives beside .venv, not in it. The prefix is about the terminal.

  • The prefix means the environment is active, so python and later pip use .venv.

  • The environment is built from a global Python, so one must be installed.

Show answer

B. The prefix means the environment is active, so python and later pip use .venv.

3The command VS Code typed was /usr/bin/python3 /Users/sam/python-projects/hello.py. Is the project's .venv being used?

  • The first path names the interpreter. A .venv interpreter's path would contain .venv.

  • Where the file lives doesn't decide which Python runs it. The first path does.

Show answer

A. The first path names the interpreter. A .venv interpreter's path would contain .venv.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Lay out python-projects so every module's files are easy to find.
  • Name files in a way that never clashes with Python's own modules.
  • Read a traceback from the bottom up to find the line and the cause.
  • Use a four-step routine (read, locate, inspect, shrink) before asking for help.

Here's a bug that has nothing to do with your code. You write a dice game, save it as random.py, and run it. Python replies:

When your program says import random, Python looks in your project folder first. It finds your own random.py, imports that instead of the real one, and your file has no randint. Recent versions of Python (3.13 and newer) spell out the fix, as you can see: rename the file. Older versions print only the first half of that message, which is far more confusing. A few habits about folders and names prevent this and most other "it worked yesterday" problems.

#One folder per module

Keep everything under the python-projects folder you opened last lesson, with a subfolder for each module. After a few modules it will look like this:

The one .venv at the top serves every module, so you only build it once. The scratch folder is for quick experiments you don't mean to keep. Drag hello.py and check_setup.py into m1-setup now; VS Code's Explorer lets you drag files between folders. Each Practice lesson gets a practice folder with one file per exercise (ex1_word_count.py, ex2_tags.py, and so on), so you can come back to any of them.

Rules for file names that save you trouble:

  • Lowercase letters, digits, and underscores only: grade_book.py, not Grade Book.py. A file you might import one day can't have spaces or dashes in its name.
  • Start with a letter.
  • Never reuse the name of something you import. json.py, random.py, math.py, test.py, and string.py are the usual culprits.

💡 Tip

To rename a file, right-click it in VS Code's Explorer and choose Rename (or select it and press F2 on Windows and Linux, Enter on a Mac). You may also notice a __pycache__ folder appear next to your files: Python keeps quick-loading copies of imported files there. It's safe to ignore or delete.

#Save, run, look, repeat

Small loops beat big ones. Write two or three lines, run, check the output, then write the next two. When something breaks you know it's in the last few lines you touched.

A few terminal habits make that loop fast:

  • Up arrow brings back the last command, so re-running is two keystrokes.
  • Ctrl+C stops a program that is stuck, for example in a loop that never ends. It works on a Mac too (Ctrl, not Cmd).
  • clear wipes the terminal so new output isn't mixed with old errors.
  • Turn on File → Auto Save if you haven't. Most "my fix didn't work" moments are an unsaved file.

VS Code also checks your code as you type. A red wavy underline usually marks a line that will fail, such as a misspelled name or a missing bracket, and a yellow one is a warning. Hover over it to read the message, or open the Problems panel from View → Problems to see them all at once.

#How to use the code on these pages

Every code block that shows output underneath has really been run, and the output is exactly what Python printed. When a lesson asks you to predict the output, make your guess before looking. Being wrong on a guess you committed to teaches you more than reading the right answer.

Type the examples into your own files instead of pasting them. Your fingers learn the syntax, and you'll make small typos that teach you what real error messages look like. In Practice lessons, give each exercise an honest ten minutes, then open the hint, and only then the solution. Comparing your version with the solution is where a lot of the learning happens, so do it even when yours works.

#Read a traceback from the bottom up

When a program crashes, Python prints a traceback: the story of which line called which, ending at the line that failed. Predict what happens when this runs:

Ava's line prints fine, then the program crashes on Ben. Read the traceback in this order:

  1. The last line says what went wrong: ZeroDivisionError: division by zero. The word before the colon is the error type; the rest is the message.
  2. The frame just above it says where: line 2, the return inside average. The ~~~^~~~ marks underneath underline the expression that failed, with the ^ under the / that did the dividing.
  3. The frames above that say how you got there: the bottom-level code called report("Ben", []), which called average([]).

So the cause isn't really line 2. Line 2 is fine for any list with something in it. The cause is that report passed an empty list along without checking. That's a common pattern: the line that crashes is the messenger, and the real decision to fix is a frame or two higher.

#The four-step routine for getting unstuck

The third step is the one people skip. Don't guess what a variable holds; ask Python. Printing with repr() shows hidden characters, and type() shows what kind of value you have:

Plain print hides the newline at the end of "42\n", so the first line looks innocent and the output has a strange blank gap. repr shows the \n plainly. Values read from files and from input() are full of surprises like this, and Module 4 will run into exactly this one.

If you're still stuck after shrinking, ask for help with four things: what you expected, what happened instead, the full error text, and the smallest piece of code that shows the problem. Questions like that get answered quickly, and half the time you solve it yourself while writing them down.

#Tracebacks on video

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A traceback's last line is KeyError: 'email'. What is the best first move?

  • You haven't found the problem yet. Rewriting without understanding often keeps the bug.

  • The error says a key is missing. Printing the dictionary shows which keys it really has.

  • A KeyError comes from your data, not from a broken installation.

Show answer

B. The error says a key is missing. Printing the dictionary shows which keys it really has.

2You save a file as json.py, and json.dump(...) fails with AttributeError. Why?

  • It's still there. The problem is which json got imported.

  • Your project folder is searched first, so your file hides the standard library one. Rename it.

  • VS Code has nothing to do with it. Any editor would give the same error.

Show answer

B. Your project folder is searched first, so your file hides the standard library one. Rename it.

3A program is stuck printing the same line over and over. How do you stop it?

  • Ctrl+C interrupts the running program on every system, Mac included.

  • That saves the file. The program keeps running.

  • The program runs in the terminal, not in the tab, so it carries on.

Show answer

A. Ctrl+C interrupts the running program on every system, Mac included.

  • Errors and Exceptions (opens in a new tab): the official tutorial's chapter on what tracebacks contain and how exceptions work.
  • Basic editing in VS Code (opens in a new tab): Auto Save, multiple cursors, and other editor habits worth picking up early.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Keep each record's fields together in a dictionary, and many records in a list.
  • Choose between a list, dict, set, and tuple based on the question you'll ask of the data.
  • Read and change values deep inside nested structures, and loop over them.
  • Build new lists and dicts with comprehensions.
  • Sort records by any field with sorted(..., key=...).

Here's a grade book that lies. It keeps names in one list and scores in another, matched by position. Then it sorts the scores so the best is first:

Cleo got the 95, not Ava. Sorting moved the scores but not the names, so the two lists no longer line up. Lists that are matched only by position stay matched only until one of them changes. The fix is to stop splitting a record across two lists.

#Keep each record together

A dictionary stores values under names called keys. One dictionary per student keeps the name and score welded together, and a list holds all the students in order:

Now max hands back the whole record, so the name can't drift away from the score. (The key= part tells max what to compare; it gets its own section below.) Notice the two kinds of brackets: students[1] picks the second item of the list by position, and ["name"] picks a value from that dictionary by key.

Dictionaries are easy to change. Assigning to a new key adds it, and assigning to an existing key replaces the value:

ava["email"] would crash with KeyError: 'email'. When a key might be missing, check with in or use .get(key, default), which returns the default instead of crashing.

#Choose the collection by the question you'll ask

Python has four everyday collections, and the right one depends on how you'll use the data, not on what the data is.

If you need to… Use a Example
Keep items in order, duplicates allowed list ["worksheet 4", "lab report"]
Look a value up by a name or ID dict {"MATH": "Algebra II", "BIO": "Biology"}
Keep only unique items and test membership quickly set {"math", "exam"}
Bundle a fixed group of values that belong together tuple ("2026-11-20", "09:00")

A set throws duplicates away the moment you build it. Sets have no fixed order, so print them through sorted() when the order matters to a reader. A tuple can't be changed after it's made, and day, time = due unpacks it into two variables in one line.

#Reach into nested data

Real data nests: a planner holds courses, each course holds tasks. Read a chain of brackets left to right, one level per bracket:

planner["courses"] is a dict of courses, ["MATH"] is one course (another dict), ["tasks"] is its list, and [-1] is the last task. .items() gives you each key and value together, which is what you almost always want when looping over a dict.

The loop inside a loop is the part people misread. The inner loop runs all the way through for each single pass of the outer loop. Step through it and watch total reset for each student:

#Comprehensions build new lists

A lot of loops have the same shape: start with an empty list, loop, maybe test something, append. A comprehension writes that whole shape in one line:

Read [s + 5 for s in scores] as "give me s + 5, for each s in scores." The optional if at the end filters: items that fail the test are skipped. Here is the loop that a filtering comprehension stands for. Step through it, then compare with the one-liner on its last line:

Comprehensions work on records too, and with curly braces they build dictionaries. Combined with string methods they turn messy text into clean data:

raw.split(",") cuts the text at each comma, .strip() trims spaces from both ends, and .lower() makes "Math" and "math" the same tag. ", ".join(...) goes the other way, gluing a list of strings into one. Keep comprehensions short. If one needs two ifs and a nested loop, a regular loop is easier to read.

#Sort by any field with key=

sorted(students) alone crashes, because Python has no idea how to compare one dictionary with another. You tell it with key=: a function that takes one item and returns the value to compare.

lambda s: s["score"] is a tiny unnamed function: given a student, return their score. In the second sort the key returns a tuple. Tuples compare item by item, so students are ordered by -score first (highest first, because the scores are negated) and ties are broken by name. Dev and Ava both have 88. In the first list Dev comes first only because he was typed first; with the tuple key, ties always come out alphabetically.

sorted() returns a new list and leaves the original alone. A list's own .sort() method rearranges the list in place and returns None, which leads straight to the most common sorting bug:

⚠️ Watch out

names = names.sort() sorts the list, then replaces it with None, the value .sort() returns. The crash comes a line later: TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable. Either call names.sort() on its own line, or write names = sorted(names).

⚠️ Watch out

Passing key=score_of() with parentheses calls the function immediately, with no student to work on. Pass the function itself, key=score_of, and sorted will call it once per item.

#Another walk through comprehensions

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does [n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3, 4] if n % 2 == 0] give?

  • That doubles every number. The if keeps only the even ones first.

  • Only 2 and 4 pass n % 2 == 0, and each is doubled.

  • Those are the numbers that pass the filter, but the comprehension outputs n * 2.

Show answer

B. Only 2 and 4 pass n % 2 == 0, and each is doubled.

2A check-in desk needs to answer "has this student arrived yet?" thousands of times. Which collection fits best for the arrived students?

  • It works, but in has to scan the list item by item, and duplicates can creep in.

  • Sets keep each item once and answer in almost instantly, however big they get.

  • Tuples can't change, and students keep arriving.

Show answer

B. Sets keep each item once and answer in almost instantly, however big they get.

3With the planner from this page, what is planner["courses"]["BIO"]["tasks"][0]?

  • BIO's task list starts with "lab report", and [0] is the first item.

  • That is the value under "title", not the first task.

  • That is MATH's first task. The ["BIO"] step chooses a different course.

Show answer

A. BIO's task list starts with "lab report", and [0] is the first item.

4order = [3, 1, 2].sort(). What is order?

  • The list does get sorted, but the variable doesn't receive it.

  • .sort() changes a list in place and returns None. Use sorted([3, 1, 2]) to get a new list back.

Show answer

B. .sort() changes a list in place and returns None. Use sorted([3, 1, 2]) to get a new list back.

Key takeaways

  • Keep a record's fields together in a dict, and a group of records in a list.
  • Lists for order, dicts for lookup by key, sets for uniqueness, tuples for fixed bundles.
  • Read nested brackets left to right, one level each; the inner loop finishes before the outer one advances.
  • [expr for item in items if test] builds a list; {k: v for ...} builds a dict.
  • sorted(items, key=...) returns a new list ordered by whatever the key function returns; .sort() returns None.

#Further reading

  • Data Structures (opens in a new tab): the official tutorial on lists, comprehensions, tuples, sets, and dictionaries, with short examples of each method.
  • Sorting Techniques (opens in a new tab): the Python docs' guide to key=, sorting on several fields, and why Python's sort keeps ties in their original order.

m2-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn lines of comma-separated text into a list of clean dictionaries.
  • Group records into a dictionary of lists, keyed by student.
  • Compute averages with a dict comprehension and rank them with sorted(key=...).
  • Find the top scorer in each subject with max(..., key=...).
  • Print a lined-up report using f-string widths.

A teacher exports a class's scores from a spreadsheet and pastes the text into a message. Somebody typed some of it by hand, so it's a little messy. Your job is to turn it into a ranked report with averages and letter grades, without fixing the data by hand. Here's the plan, and the shape the data takes at each stage:

Make a folder m2-gradebook and a file gradebook.py inside it. Each step below adds code to the bottom of that file. Run the file after every step and check that you see what the page shows.

#Step 1: Look at the raw data

Module 4 shows how to read text like this from a file. For now it lives in a multi-line string, which starts and ends with three quote marks:

Thirteen lines: one header and twelve scores. repr exposes the mess in line 6: a lowercase name with a trailing space and a score with a leading space. Look closer at the raw text and you'll spot two more problems: Science has a capital letter, and Dev's science score is blank. A good parser handles all of that.

#Step 2: Parse one line into a record

Write the cleanup for a single line first. It's much easier to test one line than twelve:

The comprehension splits the line and strips every piece in one go. Then .title() turns ben into Ben, .lower() turns Science into science, and int() turns the text "68" into the number 68. When a line doesn't have three pieces, or the score is empty, the function returns None to mean "not a usable record" instead of crashing on int("").

#Step 3: Parse every line, and keep a list of rejects

lines[1:] is every line except the header. You could build records with a comprehension, but this loop also collects the rejected lines. Throwing bad data away silently is how grade books end up wrong without anyone noticing. Keeping the rejects means the report can say what it ignored.

#Step 4: Group the scores by student

To average each student you need all of their scores together. A dictionary whose values are lists does that:

The first time a name shows up, it gets an empty list; every time after that, the score is appended to the list that's already there. This "group into a dict of lists" pattern comes up constantly. Python even has a shortcut for the middle three lines, by_student.setdefault(name, []).append(record["score"]), which you'll see in the final program.

#Step 5: Averages and letter grades

A dict comprehension turns each list into its average. .items() hands over each name with its list:

Dev's average comes from two scores, not three, because his blank science score was skipped. That's a decision worth making on purpose. The alternative, counting a missing score as zero, would drag his average from 68.5 down to 45.7 for a test that may simply not have been entered yet.

#Step 6: Rank the students

Sorting averages.items() gives a list of (name, average) pairs. The key returns (-average, name), so the highest average comes first and ties are broken alphabetically:

pair[1] is the average and pair[0] is the name. The comprehension on the last line unpacks each pair into two variables and keeps just the names, which is a quick way to check the order.

#Step 7: Top scorer in each subject

The teacher also wants the best score in each subject. That's a different grouping: a dict of subjects, each holding a dict of names to scores.

max(scores, key=scores.get) is worth reading slowly. Looping over a dict gives its keys (the names), and key=scores.get tells max to compare each name by the score stored under it. The result is the name with the highest score, which you then use to look the score up.

#Step 8: Print a report that lines up

An f-string can pad a value to a width: :<6 left-aligns in 6 characters, :>6.1f right-aligns a number in 6 characters with one decimal place.

enumerate(ranking, start=1) numbers the pairs from 1, and (name, average) unpacks each pair right in the for line.

#The finished program

Here's everything tidied into functions, each with one job, plus a main() that runs them in order. Replace the contents of gradebook.py with it:

Two things changed on the way. group_scores now takes the field to group by, so the same function makes both the per-student and per-subject groups. And letter loops over a list of (cutoff, grade) tuples, so changing the grading scale means editing one list instead of a chain of ifs.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does parse_line return None for Dev's blank science score instead of calling int() on it?

  • It doesn't return 0; it crashes with ValueError.

  • Returning None lets the caller skip the line and list it at the end.

  • It can: int("68") gives 68. Only text that isn't a number fails.

Show answer

B. Returning None lets the caller skip the line and list it at the end.

2In sorted(averages.items(), key=lambda pair: (-pair[1], pair[0])), why the minus sign?

  • reverse=True would flip the names too. Negating only the average flips just that part.

  • A minus sign changes the sign, not the type. -87.5 is still a float.

  • It handles any numbers; the minus sign is about direction.

Show answer

A. reverse=True would flip the names too. Negating only the average flips just that part.

3What does max(scores, key=scores.get) return when scores = {"Ava": 91, "Ben": 68}?

  • max loops over the dict's keys, so it returns a key. 91 is the value stored under it.

  • Each name is compared by scores.get(name), and Ava's 91 is the largest.

  • That would need max(scores.items(), ...). A plain dict gives just keys.

Show answer

B. Each name is compared by scores.get(name), and Ava's 91 is the largest.

Key takeaways

  • Write and test the code for one line before you loop over all of them.
  • Keep rejected input in its own list so the program can report what it ignored.
  • "Dict of lists" is the standard way to group records; setdefault shortens it.
  • A key that returns a tuple sorts on several things at once; negate a number to flip just that part.
  • f-string widths such as :<6 and :>6.1f line up columns without counting spaces.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a weight for each subject (say, math counts double) and compute weighted averages.
  • Print each student's lowest subject next to their average.
  • Count how many students got each letter grade, using a dict of counts.
  • Show subjects in order of class average, hardest first.

#Further reading

  • String methods (opens in a new tab): every method you can call on text, including split, strip, title, and join.
  • Format specification mini-language (opens in a new tab): the full list of what can go after the colon in an f-string, from widths to thousands separators.
  • The csv module (opens in a new tab): for real spreadsheet exports, where a value might itself contain a comma inside quotes, use this instead of split(",").

Write down what you think each line prints, then run it:

Count how often each word appears in this text, ignoring capital letters and the punctuation . , ! ?. Print the three most common words with their counts, breaking ties alphabetically.

Expected output:

#Exercise 2: Every tag, once

Each task has a list of tags. Print all the different tags in alphabetical order, then how many tasks use each one.

Expected output:

#Exercise 3: What's urgent?

From the list below, print the titles of tasks that are not done and due within 3 days (due_in <= 3), soonest first.

Expected output:

Need a hint?

One comprehension with an if that checks two things joined by and. Then sort the result with key=lambda t: t["due_in"], and finally pull out just the titles.

#Exercise 4: Sort contacts by last name

Sort these names by last name, then by first name, ignoring capital letters. Print one per line, exactly as they were typed.

Expected output:

Need a hint?

Write a small function last_then_first(full_name) that lowercases the name, splits it into first and last, and returns the tuple (last, first). Pass the function itself, without parentheses, as key=.

Show solution

The key only decides the order; it never changes what's in the list. That's why ava patel still prints in lowercase. Without .lower(), she'd jump to the end, because Python sorts all capital letters before all lowercase ones.

#Exercise 5: Flip the dictionary

You have each student's clubs. The club advisors want the opposite: for each club, its members. Build that dictionary and print the clubs alphabetically.

Expected output:

Need a hint?

Every arrow in the diagram is one pass of a nested loop: outer loop over clubs_by_student.items(), inner loop over that student's clubs. For each pair, append the student to the club's list, creating the list the first time you see the club.

setdefault(club, []) returns the club's existing list, or puts in an empty one and returns that. Either way .append(student) has a list to work on. The members come out in alphabetical order only because the students were typed that way; add sorted() around each list if you need to be sure.

#Exercise 6: Study log totals

Each entry in the log is a (day, subject, minutes) tuple. Print the total minutes for each day as a dict, then the busiest day and the most-studied subject.

Expected output:

Need a hint?

Unpack each tuple right in the loop: for day, subject, minutes in log:. Keep two dicts of running totals, and update both in the same pass. max(totals, key=totals.get) finds the key with the biggest value.

Show solution

One loop fills both dictionaries because each log entry contributes to a day and a subject. Tuples suit the log well: each entry is a fixed bundle of three values that nobody should edit after the fact.

#Challenge: A study planner's data model

Design the data for a study planner, then write three functions for it:

  • Courses must be looked up by code ("MATH"), tasks inside a course kept in the order they were added, and each task's tags stored without duplicates.
  • add_task(planner, code, title, due, tags) adds a not-done task and returns True, or returns False if the course code doesn't exist. Store due as text like "2026-11-18".

A dict of courses, each holding a list of task dicts, each with a set of tags. Dates written year-month-day sort correctly as plain text, so a tuple that starts with due sorts by date for free. min() of a list of tuples gives the soonest.

Show solution

What you'll learn

  • Trace a loop inside a loop with conditions at each level.
  • Flatten deep nesting with guard clauses (continue and early return).
  • Explain why a function that prints instead of returning gives back None.
  • Split a tangled function into small functions that each do one job.
  • Predict when a variable is local or global, and fix UnboundLocalError.

This report generator prints the right totals for every active team, and then gets the one thing you actually wanted wrong:

"Best team: None." Two separate things went wrong. The function prints its results instead of handing them back, so the caller receives nothing. And the logic that matters is buried four indents deep, which makes it hard to see where a "best team" calculation would even go. This lesson fixes both.

#Read nested code from the inside out

Deeply nested code is easiest to understand starting from the innermost line and working outward. In report:

  • The innermost if decides which players count: only those who played a game.
  • The player loop adds those players' points into total.
  • The if team["active"] decides which teams get a total at all.
  • The outer loop repeats all of that once per team.

Notice that total = 0 sits inside the team loop, so every team starts from zero. Step through a smaller version and watch it reset. The players here are (games, points) tuples to keep the trace short:

For the Owls, the if is false, so the whole inner block is skipped and nothing prints. Every extra level of nesting is another condition you have to hold in your head while reading the lines below it.

#Guard clauses: deal with the exceptions first

A guard clause checks for a case you don't want to handle and gets out early. In a loop, continue skips to the next item. In a function, return leaves right away. The main work then sits at the left margin instead of at the bottom of a staircase.

Compare two versions of the same ticket-price rule:

Both give identical answers, but the guarded one reads like the rule you'd say out loud: "Negative ages are invalid. Under-fives are free. Members pay 6. Everyone else pays 10." Each special case is handled and forgotten, one line at a time.

The same idea flattens the team loop:

To write a guard, flip the condition: if team["active"]: becomes if not team["active"]: continue.

#Return the answer, and let the caller decide what to print

print shows a value to a person, and then the value is gone. return hands the value back to the code that called the function, which can store it, compare it, sort by it, or print it. A function with no return statement still returns something: None. That's what best received in the opening example.

total_printed displays 21, but a is None, so a * 2 would crash with TypeError. b is a real number you can keep working with. A useful rule: functions that calculate should return; only a few functions near the top of the program should talk to the user with print and input.

A function can return several values at once by returning a tuple, which the caller unpacks:

#Small functions with one job each

Now rebuild the report from small pieces. Each function has a name that says what it gives back, takes everything it needs as parameters, and returns its answer:

Look at what small functions buy you. team_total is one line you can check by eye. (The sum(points for ... if ...) inside it is a comprehension without the square brackets; it feeds each value straight into sum instead of building a list first.) Each piece can be tested on its own with assert, which does nothing when the claim is true and crashes loudly when it's false. And best_team was easy to add, because the totals now exist as a value instead of scrolling past on the screen.

#Where variables live: scope

A variable created inside a function is local: it exists only while that call is running, and the caller can't see it. A variable created at the top level of the file is global, and functions can read it. The trap is assigning to a global name inside a function:

Because add_point assigns to count, Python decides that count is local for the whole function. So when the right-hand side tries to read count, the local one doesn't exist yet. The fix is the same habit as before: pass values in and return results out.

Python does have a global statement that lets a function reassign a global, but code built on it is hard to test and hard to follow, because any function might be changing any variable. Parameters and return values keep each function's inputs and outputs in plain sight.

⚠️ Watch out

A return in the wrong place ends the loop early. This checker is meant to report whether any score is failing:

has_failing([80, 45]) returns False, because the else returns on the very first score. A function can only conclude "none of them" after checking all of them, so the return False belongs after the loop, unindented.

⚠️ Watch out

Reading a local from outside. After team_total(team) runs, writing print(total) at the top level gives NameError: name 'total' is not defined if total was only created inside a function. Capture the result instead: total = team_total(team).

#print and return, side by side

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does this print? def shout(word): print(word.upper()) then x = shout("hi") then print(x)

  • The function prints once, but it never returns the text, so x can't hold it.

  • Calling shout prints HI. With no return, the call's value is None, which is then printed.

  • The print inside the function still runs when it's called.

Show answer

B. Calling shout prints HI. With no return, the call's value is None, which is then printed.

2Which line is a guard clause?

  • It handles a special case (an empty list) and leaves, so the rest of the function can assume there are scores.

  • That's the main work, not a check that leaves early.

  • Returning at the end is normal; a guard returns early on a special case.

Show answer

A. It handles a special case (an empty list) and leaves, so the rest of the function can assume there are scores.

3Why does count = count + 1 inside a function crash with UnboundLocalError when count exists globally?

  • They can read them. The problem only starts when the function also assigns to the name.

  • Python decides scope before the function runs. A local count has no value yet when the right side needs it.

  • Rebinding a name to a new integer is fine; this is about which count the name refers to.

Show answer

B. Python decides scope before the function runs. A local count has no value yet when the right side needs it.

4A function team_report(team) calculates a total and prints a formatted line. What's the best way to split it?

  • It still mixes calculating and displaying, so you can't reuse the total without printing.

  • Each piece has one job, can be tested with assert, and can be reused elsewhere.

  • Globals hide where values come from. Return values make the data flow visible.

Show answer

B. Each piece has one job, can be tested with assert, and can be reused elsewhere.

Key takeaways

  • Read nested code from the innermost line outward; each level adds a condition to keep in mind.
  • Guard clauses (continue, early return) handle special cases first and keep the main path flat.
  • print shows a value and loses it; return hands it back. No return means the call gives None.
  • Functions that calculate should return; leave printing and input to a few functions at the top.
  • Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local everywhere in that function. Pass values in and return them out.

#Further reading

  • Defining functions (opens in a new tab): the official tutorial on def, return, and what a function gives back when it has no return.
  • Why am I getting an UnboundLocalError? (opens in a new tab): the Python FAQ's short, exact explanation of the scope rule behind this crash.
  • The Zen of Python (opens in a new tab): nineteen one-line design rules, including "Flat is better than nested."

What you'll learn

  • Plan a program as a set of small functions before writing any of them.
  • Clean and check input with guard clauses that return early.
  • Return values and messages instead of printing them inside helpers.
  • Change a list passed into a function, and explain why the caller sees the change.
  • Keep all input() and menu printing in one main() function.

You're building a contacts manager that runs in the terminal. You'll be able to add people, search by name, email, or part of a phone number, list everyone, and delete people. It will also refuse bad data politely: a phone number with seven digits or an email with no dot after the @ gets an explanation, not a crash.

The design rule for this build comes straight from the last lesson: helpers calculate and return; only main() talks to the user. Here's the plan:

Make a folder m3-contacts and a file contacts.py. Add each step's code to the bottom of the file and run it as you go.

#Step 1: Decide what a contact looks like

Before writing functions, settle the data. Each contact is a dictionary, and all contacts live in one list:

Notice the phone is stored as digits only, as text. People type numbers as 415-555-0123, (415) 555-0123, or +1 415 555 0123. Storing one clean form means searching and comparing never have to worry about dashes and brackets. It's text, not an int, because a phone number is a label you never do math on, and some begin with 0.

#Step 2: Clean up phone numbers

normalize_phone keeps only the digit characters, drops a leading country code 1, and then uses a guard clause: anything that isn't exactly ten digits returns None. It doesn't print "invalid phone". The function can't know whether the caller wants to show a message, try again, or skip the record, so it reports the fact and lets the caller decide. The assert lines are tiny tests; leave them in while you build, and they'll shout if a later change breaks something.

#Step 3: A sanity check for email addresses

Fully checking an email address is surprisingly hard (the official rules run to pages). This version only catches obvious typos, which is all a contacts list needs:

Each guard throws out one kind of mistake. Once a line has survived the guards, the code below it can safely assume there is exactly one @ and a non-empty name before it. The last line returns the result of a test directly, instead of writing if ...: return True else: return False.

#Step 4: Format one contact for display

This returns a string rather than printing it. That means a search result, a full list, or a future "export to file" feature can all reuse it. The dictionary keys use single quotes because the f-string itself uses double quotes.

#Step 5: Add a contact, with guard clauses

add_contact returns a pair: did it work, and a message explaining what happened. The four guards run in order, and the first problem found is the one reported. Only a contact that passes all of them reaches contacts.append(...) at the bottom.

Here's the part that surprises people: add_contact never returns the list, yet book grew. When you pass a list to a function, the function gets the same list, not a copy. Appending inside the function changes the one list both names refer to. That's useful here, but it's also why a helper should only change a list when changing it is the whole point of the function, as its name says.

#Step 6: Search

One comprehension checks three things, joined with or. The phone check is wrapped in (digits and ...) so a query with no digits, such as "chen", doesn't count as matching every phone number (every string contains the empty string). Results come back sorted, and an empty list means no matches, which the caller can handle however it likes.

#Step 7: Delete

enumerate gives each contact's position so del contacts[index] can remove it. The function returns immediately after deleting. Carrying on with a loop over a list you've just shortened makes Python skip the item that slid into the gap. And return False sits after the loop, so it only runs once every contact has been checked.

#Step 8: The menu, the only part that talks

main is all conversation: it asks, calls a helper, and prints what came back. Choosing q uses return to leave the while True loop and end the program. Any choice that isn't on the menu falls through to the final else instead of being silently ignored.

#The finished program

Here's the whole contacts.py, with the tests removed. This run tries everything, including a bad email, a search by phone digits, a delete, and a menu choice that doesn't exist:

Every contact disappears when the program ends, because contacts only lives in memory. Module 4 fixes that by saving the list to a JSON file.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does normalize_phone return None for a bad number instead of printing "Invalid phone"?

  • Functions can print; it's a design choice, not a rule of the language.

  • add_contact turns None into a message; a file importer could skip the row instead. An assert can check None directly.

  • The difference is negligible. The reason is who gets to decide what happens next.

Show answer

B. add_contact turns None into a message; a file importer could skip the row instead. An assert can check None directly.

2add_contact(book, ...) never returns book, but afterwards book has a new contact. Why?

  • add_contact never mentions book. It changes whatever list it was given.

  • Passing a list doesn't copy it, so the parameter contacts and the caller's book are two names for one list.

  • It doesn't. add_contact returns the (ok, message) pair and nothing else.

Show answer

B. Passing a list doesn't copy it, so the parameter contacts and the caller's book are two names for one list.

3Why does delete_contact return straight after del contacts[index]?

  • Deleting shifts later items left by one, so the loop would jump over the next contact.

  • del works anywhere. The early return is about the loop, not about del.

  • The early return True ends the function, so return False doesn't run at all in that case.

Show answer

A. Deleting shifts later items left by one, so the loop would jump over the next contact.

Key takeaways

  • Sketch the functions and the data before writing code; decide which single function talks to the user.
  • Guard clauses in helpers reject bad input early and return a value that explains why.
  • Return pairs like (ok, message) when the caller needs both a result and an explanation.
  • A list passed into a function is shared, not copied, so changes inside are visible outside.
  • After deleting from a list inside a loop, stop looping (return) or you'll skip items.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add an edit option that changes one contact's phone or email, reusing normalize_phone and is_valid_email.
  • Let each contact have a set of groups ("family", "team") and search by group.
  • List contacts by last name using the sort key from Module 2's practice.
  • Ask "Are you sure?" before deleting, inside main() where the conversation belongs.

#Further reading

  • More on defining functions (opens in a new tab): default parameter values, keyword arguments, and the warning about using a list as a default value.
  • PEP 8: function and variable names (opens in a new tab): Python's style guide on naming, including why find_contacts beats fc or FindContacts.
  • The assert statement (opens in a new tab): exactly what assert does, and why it isn't a replacement for real input checks.

What does the last line print? Decide before running it.

double works out 8 and then throws it away, because nothing returns it. A line like n * 2 on its own is legal Python, which is why this bug never produces an error message of its own.

#Exercise 1: The average that isn't there

This program crashes. Fix average so the if works, and make it return 0 for an empty list instead of crashing on division by zero. Then print a status for each list of scores.

Expected output once fixed, for the lists [72, 81, 64], [55, 61], and []:

Need a hint?

The error message names NoneType: something that should be a number is None. Replace print with return. Add a guard clause as the first line of the function for the empty list.

if not scores is true for an empty list, so the guard returns before the division can fail. Returning 0 is a choice; returning None would be more honest ("there's no average"), but then every caller must check for None before comparing.

#Exercise 2: Flatten the staircase

Rewrite this function with guard clauses so no line is indented more than once inside the function. It must give the same message for every input.

Test it with these cases:

Need a hint?

Find each else and the if it belongs to. Flip that if's condition (has_form becomes not has_form) and return the else message straight away. Keep the checks in the same order, because the order decides which message wins when several things are wrong.

Write three functions for a school-store receipt: subtotal(items) returns the cost before tax, tax(amount, rate) returns the tax rounded to cents, and format_receipt(items, rate) returns the whole receipt as one string. Only the last line of the program should print.

Expected output:

Need a hint?

Build a list of lines, one string each, then return "\n".join(lines). format_receipt should call subtotal and tax rather than repeating their math. Check the first two functions with assert before formatting anything.

Because format_receipt returns a string, the same receipt could be emailed, saved to a file in Module 4, or compared in a test, all without touching the math.

#Exercise 4: The high score that won't update

Run this and read the error. Then rewrite record so it takes the current high score as a parameter and returns the new one. The program should print 75.

Need a hint?

The assignment high_score = score makes high_score local to record everywhere in that function, including the if line above it. Give the function a second parameter, return whichever score is higher, and assign the result back in the loop.

Show solution

Now record has no hidden connection to the outside: the current best comes in, the new best goes out. (Python's built-in max(score, high_score) does the same job, which is a good sign you've designed it sensibly.)

#Exercise 5: Find double-booked rooms

Two groups clash if they've booked the same room in the same period. Write find_clashes(bookings) that returns a list of (room, period, group_a, group_b) tuples, checking every pair of bookings exactly once.

Expected output:

To visit every pair once, the inner loop starts one position after the outer loop. Step through it with three items and watch which (i, j) pairs appear:

Need a hint?

Use for i in range(len(bookings)) and for j in range(i + 1, len(bookings)). Inside, unpack bookings[i] and bookings[j] into room, period, and group, and compare the room and period.

Show solution

Starting j at i + 1 skips comparing a booking with itself and avoids reporting each clash twice (once as A-B, once as B-A). For six bookings that's 15 comparisons. With a thousand bookings it would be about half a million, and grouping by (room, period) in a dictionary, as in Module 2, would be far quicker.

#Exercise 6: Split the sales report

Write three functions: group_by_store(sales) returns a dict of store to a list of (item, amount) pairs, where amount is quantity times price; store_summary(lines) returns (revenue, best_item); and format_report(groups) returns the report as a string, highest revenue first. Test the first two with assert.

Expected output:

Need a hint?

group_by_store is the "dict of lists" pattern with setdefault. In store_summary, max(lines, key=lambda line: line[1]) finds the pair with the biggest amount. In format_report, build a dict of summaries first, then sort its items by revenue.

Show solution

pair[1][0] reads as "the summary, then its revenue": each item of summaries.items() is (store, (revenue, best)). If that line feels cryptic, a named function def by_revenue(pair): return pair[1][0] says the same thing more clearly.

#Challenge: Rescue the attendance report

This function works, but it prints from four levels deep and nothing in it can be tested on its own. Refactor it into small functions (days_present, has_perfect_attendance, class_summary, format_summary, and an attendance_report that returns a string), add assert tests, and add one feature: each class's attendance rate as a percentage, with classes listed highest rate first. A class with no students who have any recorded days should be left out, just as it is now.

Need a hint?

Start from the innermost loop: counting "P" in a list is days.count("P"). Let class_summary return a dict (or None for a class with nothing to report), so the rate can be calculated as present days divided by possible days. An f-string format of :.0% turns 0.875 into 88%.

Show solution

The four nested levels became four functions, none more than one level deep. The guard in class_summary replaced both the outer if c["students"] and the inner if s["days"], because filtering students first means an empty class and a class of students with no days are the same case. Adding the rate needed one new line in class_summary and one change in format_summary; in the original it would have meant another variable threaded through every level.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write and read text files with with open(...), and choose the right mode.
  • Save and load whole lists and dicts with json.dump and json.load.
  • Predict what JSON changes on the way through (tuples, sets, number keys).
  • Handle a missing file and a corrupt file without crashing or destroying data.
  • Build file paths with pathlib, and save in a way that can't leave a half-written file.

An expense tracker that forgets everything is worse than a notebook. Run this twice:

It says 2 both times, never 4. Variables live in memory, which is wiped the moment the program ends. To remember something until next time, a program must write it to a file on disk and read it back when it starts.

#Write and read text with with open

open connects your program to a file. The with block closes the file for you when the block ends, even if an error happens inside it:

write adds exactly what you give it and nothing more, so you add the "\n" (newline) yourself. Leave it out and both expenses end up on one line. The file now exists beside your program. A separate program can read it back:

Looping over a file gives one line at a time, with its newline on the end, as repr shows. .strip() removes it before you split. Everything read from a text file is a string, so float(amount) is needed before any math.

The second argument to open is the mode:

Mode Means If the file exists If it doesn't
"r" (the default) read reads from the start FileNotFoundError
"w" write erases it first creates it
"a" append adds to the end creates it

"a" kept the two earlier lines and added a third. file.read() returns the whole file as one string.

⚠️ Watch out

Opening with "w" empties the file immediately, before you write a single character. If you meant to add a line and used "w", the old contents are already gone. When in doubt, read first, then write.

Always pass encoding="utf-8". Without it, some computers (especially Windows ones with older versions of Python) use a different default, and a name like "Zoë" or an emoji can crash the program or come back garbled.

#JSON: save a whole structure in one call

Your grade book and contacts are lists of dicts, and flattening those into lines by hand is tedious. JSON is a text format that looks almost exactly like Python's lists and dicts, and the json module converts in both directions:

json.dump(data, file) writes the data; indent=2 spreads it over several lines so a person can read and even edit it. Loading is one call:

What comes back is ordinary Python: a list of dicts with real numbers in them, ready to use. (json.dumps and json.loads, with an s for "string", do the same thing with a string instead of a file.)

JSON isn't Python, though, and a few things change on the round trip. Predict the second line before you run this:

True and None become JSON's true and null, and come back fine. But JSON has no tuples, so (1, 5) returns as the list [1, 5]. And JSON keys must be strings, so the key 7 comes back as "7"; back[7] would now be a KeyError. Sets are worse: JSON has nothing like them, so json.dumps({"tags": {"food"}}) stops with TypeError: Object of type set is not JSON serializable. Convert sets with sorted(tags) before saving and back with set(...) after loading.

#When the file is missing or broken

The very first time a program runs, its data file doesn't exist yet. That's normal, not an error, and the program should start with an empty list. A try block lets you handle it: Python runs the code under try, and if one of the named errors happens, it jumps to the matching except instead of crashing.

A corrupt file is a different situation. Maybe someone edited it by hand and deleted a bracket. Here's what loading one looks like:

The traceback is long because the error was raised deep inside the json module's own code. As always, read the last line first. json.JSONDecodeError tells you where parsing gave up (line 1, column 35 here, just past the trailing comma). The tempting fix is to catch it and return [], but think about what happens next: the program starts empty, the user adds one expense, and saving overwrites the broken file, along with every expense that was in it and could have been repaired by hand. Keep a copy first:

#Paths that work on every computer

That example used pathlib, the modern way to handle file locations. A Path joins folder names correctly on every system and has handy methods built in:

The / operator joins path pieces, so you never type a slash or backslash yourself. (On Windows, the first line prints as data\budget.json, with the backslash Windows uses.) mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) makes the folder, and any missing folders above it, without complaining if it already exists.

There's one trap specific to running code from VS Code. When you press Run Python File, the terminal's current folder is the folder you opened (python-projects), not the subfolder your script is in. So open("expenses.json") in m4-quiz/tracker.py looks for python-projects/expenses.json, and you get FileNotFoundError for a file you can see right there in the Explorer. The fix is to build paths from the script's own location:

__file__ is the path of the script that's running, and .parent is its folder. Now DATA_FILE points beside the script however the program is started. (This one can't run on the page, because code here doesn't come from a saved file.)

#Save so a crash can't leave half a file

If the program crashes or the battery dies halfway through writing, you're left with half a JSON file, which is a corrupt file. The safe pattern is to write a temporary file completely, then swap it into place in one step:

replace swaps the finished file in all at once, so at every moment expenses.json is either the complete old version or the complete new one. Together with the careful loader, the whole life of the data looks like this:

#Files on video

Check your understanding

4 questions

1notes.txt has 50 lines. A program runs with open("notes.txt", "w") as f: pass and ends. How many lines are left?

  • Opening in "w" mode doesn't wait for a write. It empties the file straight away.

  • "w" truncates the file the moment it opens, and nothing was written afterwards.

  • That would need "a" mode and a write.

Show answer

B. "w" truncates the file the moment it opens, and nothing was written afterwards.

2You save {1: "gold", 2: "silver"} with json.dump and load it back. What's the result?

  • JSON keys are always strings, so the numbers don't survive as numbers.

  • The keys were turned into strings on the way out and stay strings on the way back.

  • Number keys are allowed when saving; they're quietly converted. Sets are what raise TypeError.

Show answer

B. The keys were turned into strings on the way out and stay strings on the way back.

3quiz.py and questions.json are both in python-projects/m4-quiz/. Pressing Run Python File gives FileNotFoundError: 'questions.json'. Why?

  • Files can be anywhere; what matters is the folder the path is relative to.

  • Relative paths start from the current folder, not the script's folder. Path(__file__).parent / "questions.json" fixes it.

  • That would create an empty file in the wrong place, or erase the right one.

Show answer

B. Relative paths start from the current folder, not the script's folder. Path(__file__).parent / "questions.json" fixes it.

4Why save to expenses.json.tmp and then call replace instead of writing expenses.json directly?

  • It's the same amount of writing. The benefit is safety.

  • replace happens in one step, so the real file is always a complete version.

  • json.dump works with any file you've opened for writing.

Show answer

B. replace happens in one step, so the real file is always a complete version.

Key takeaways

  • Memory is wiped when a program ends; files on disk persist.
  • with open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") closes the file for you. "w" erases, "a" adds, "r" reads.
  • json.dump and json.load save and restore lists and dicts. Tuples come back as lists, number keys as strings, and sets can't be saved at all.
  • A missing file usually means "first run, start empty". A corrupt file should be backed up before anything overwrites it.
  • Use pathlib.Path, build data paths from Path(__file__).parent, and save through a temporary file plus replace.

#Further reading

  • Reading and writing files (opens in a new tab): the official tutorial section on open, modes, and saving structured data with json.
  • json: JSON encoder and decoder (opens in a new tab): the reference for dump, load, indent, and the full table of how Python types convert.
  • pathlib: object-oriented filesystem paths (opens in a new tab): every Path method, with a table matching each one to the older os functions you'll see in other people's code.

m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Store a program's content (quiz questions) in a JSON file instead of in the code.
  • Write one safe pair of helpers for reading and writing JSON, and reuse it.
  • Check every loaded record and report problems instead of crashing.
  • Keep a score history that grows each time the program runs.
  • Recover from a damaged data file without losing its contents.

Most quiz programs beginners write keep the questions inside the code, so adding a question means editing Python. This one keeps them in questions.json, which anyone can edit in VS Code, and it remembers everyone's scores in scores.json. Here's how the pieces fit:

Make a folder m4-quiz. Every step adds code to the bottom of quiz.py inside it.

💡 Tip

While you build, run the program from the terminal inside the folder: type cd m4-quiz once, then python quiz.py each time. Until Step 7 the code opens files by bare name, and the terminal's current folder decides where those files land.

#Step 1: Create the questions file

The question file is a list of objects. Each has a prompt, a list of choices, and the answer, stored as the text of the right choice rather than its position. That way, reordering or shuffling the choices can never make the answer point at the wrong one. You can type the file by hand, or run this little script once to create it:

That printout is exactly what's in the file now. Open it in VS Code: it's plain text, so adding a fourth question is just a matter of copying one block and editing it. Be careful with commas, though. JSON needs a comma between items and forbids one after the last item, and that's the most common way a hand-edited file breaks.

#Step 2: One safe way to read and write JSON

The quiz reads two files, so write the careful version once. read_json returns a pair: the data, and a warning message or None.

These two functions are the lessons of the Notes page packed into fifteen lines. A missing file quietly gives the default. A damaged file is renamed to .bak so nothing in it is lost, and the caller gets a message to show. Writing goes through a .tmp file and replace, so a crash mid-save can't leave half a file. Neither function prints, so the rest of the program decides what the user sees.

#Step 3: Check every question

A JSON file can be perfectly valid and still wrong: a question with no choices, or an answer that isn't one of the choices. A guard-clause function finds the first problem with a question, or returns None if there isn't one:

isinstance(value, list) checks what type a value is, which matters because a JSON file can hold anything. question.get("prompt") gives None instead of crashing when the key is missing. The test file shows the point of load_questions: one good question gets through, and the two bad ones become readable messages with their position in the file, which is exactly what a person needs to fix them.

#Step 4: Ask one question

ask is a "talking" function like main in the contacts manager: it prints and reads input. It keeps asking until the reply is a number in range, then returns whether the answer was right.

reply.isdigit() comes first in the and, so int(reply) only runs on text that really is digits; int("two") would crash. Python stops checking an and as soon as one side is false, which is what makes that order safe. The player types 2, but the code compares the text of choice 2 with the answer.

#Step 5: Run the whole quiz

run_quiz returns the score instead of printing it, because the next step needs to save it.

#Step 6: Remember every score

Each finished quiz adds one record to scores.json. The history is loaded, appended to, and saved straight away:

Each call to record_score starts by reading the file, so the second call sees Ava's score from the first. That's the whole trick of persistence: read at the start, write after the change. Ranking by score / total instead of raw score keeps the leaderboard fair if you add questions later.

#Step 7: Put it together in main()

main finds the data files, warns about problems, runs the quiz, and saves the result. data_folder() returns the folder the script is saved in, so the program finds its files however it's started. When there's no saved file at all (pasted into the interactive prompt, or run on this page), __file__ doesn't exist and it falls back to the current folder.

Cleo's result joins Ava's and Ben's from Step 6, because they were saved to disk.

#Step 8: Break the scores file on purpose

Simulate someone hand-editing scores.json badly, then play again:

The quiz itself runs normally. When it goes to save Dev's score, read_json finds the damage, so the program warns, keeps the damaged text in scores.json.bak, and starts a fresh history with Dev's score. Nothing crashed, and nothing was thrown away; someone can open the .bak file and repair it by hand.

#The finished program

Here's all of quiz.py. Run it from VS Code a few times, then open scores.json in the editor and watch it grow.

The last two lines are new. if __name__ == "__main__": is true only when this file is the program being run, not when another file imports it. That lets a separate test file import question_problem and check it without a quiz starting.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why store the answer as "set" instead of as the number 3?

  • A position breaks the moment the list changes order. The text of the choice moves with it.

  • JSON stores numbers fine. This is a design choice about robustness.

  • The speed difference is irrelevant here; the reason is correctness.

Show answer

A. A position breaks the moment the list changes order. The text of the choice moves with it.

2scores.json is damaged. What does the program do with it?

  • Deleting would throw away every score that could have been repaired.

  • The data is kept for a person to fix, and the quiz still works.

  • read_json catches that error. Crashing every launch would make the quiz unusable until someone fixed the file.

Show answer

B. The data is kept for a person to fix, and the quiz still works.

3In if reply.isdigit() and 1 <= int(reply) <= len(choices), what happens when the player types two?

  • It never runs: isdigit() is false, so Python skips the rest of the and.

  • and stops at the first false part, which is why the safe check comes first.

Show answer

B. and stops at the first false part, which is why the safe check comes first.

Key takeaways

  • Keep content such as questions in a data file so it can change without touching code.
  • Write one careful read_json / write_json pair and reuse it for every file.
  • Valid JSON can still be wrong data. Check each record and report problems by position.
  • Persistence is "read at the start, write after the change"; save immediately, not only on exit.
  • if __name__ == "__main__": main() runs the program only when the file is run directly.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Shuffle the question order with random.shuffle(questions), and the choices inside each question too.
  • Add a "topic" field and let the player choose a topic before starting.
  • Show each player's personal best next to their new score.
  • Write a second program, add_question.py, that asks for a prompt, choices, and answer, checks them with question_problem, and appends the question to questions.json.

#Further reading

  • JSON syntax (opens in a new tab): the whole JSON format on one page, with diagrams of what counts as a valid value. Useful when a hand-edited file won't load.
  • Path.replace (opens in a new tab): the official description of the rename-over-an-existing-file step that makes saving safe.
  • __main__: top-level code environment (opens in a new tab): what __name__ == "__main__" really checks, with examples.

Save these in m4-quiz/practice/, and run them from a terminal inside that folder (cd m4-quiz/practice) so the files they create land beside them. Open those files in VS Code's Explorer after running; seeing what's really on disk is the fastest way to understand what your code did.

Four with blocks, three modes. Predict the output before running:

#Exercise 1: A numbered journal

Write read_entries(path), which returns the file's lines without their newlines (or [] if the file doesn't exist yet), and add_entry(path, text), which appends one line numbered after the existing ones. Start from no file and add three entries.

Expected output:

Need a hint?

add_entry can call read_entries to count the lines already there. Use mode "a" to add to the end, and remember the "\n". To start clean each time you test, Path("journal.txt").unlink(missing_ok=True) deletes the file if it exists.
