rstrip("\n") removes only the newline at the end, so spaces the user typed stay as they were. Run the program again without the unlink line and the entries continue at 4: the file remembers.

#Exercise 2: Measure a file

Save the poem below to poem.txt, then write file_stats(path) that returns a tuple of the number of lines, the number of words, and the longest line.

Expected output:

Need a hint?

Read the lines into a list first, since you need to look at them more than once. A line's word count is len(line.split()). max(lines, key=len) finds the longest line, but it crashes on an empty list, so guard against an empty file.

Show solution

A file can only be looped over once per open; after the loop, the reading position is at the end. Saving the lines in a list lets you count words and find the longest line from the same data.

#Exercise 3: The level that disappeared

A game saves how many stars you earned on each level. After loading, asking for level 2 crashes. Run it, read the error, then write save_progress and load_progress so that loaded["stars"][2] works.

Expected output once fixed:

Need a hint?

Open progress.json in VS Code and look at the keys: they have quotes around them now. After loading, rebuild the stars dict with a dict comprehension that converts each key with int().

Show solution

KeyError: 2 meant "there's no key that is the number 2", which was true: the key was the string "2". Putting the conversion inside load_progress means the rest of the program never has to know JSON was involved.

#Exercise 4: Save the planner, sets and all

The study planner from Module 2's challenge stores each task's tags as a set. Saving it crashes, and the crash does something worse than crash. Run this, then run the cell after it to see what was left on disk:

json.dump writes to the file piece by piece, so by the time it reached the set, half the planner was already on disk. The file is now corrupt. Write save_planner(path, planner), which turns each task's tags into a sorted list before saving, and load_planner(path), which turns them back into sets, so that the loaded planner equals the original.

Need a hint?

In save_planner, build a new structure instead of changing the planner you were given: dict(task, tags=sorted(task["tags"])) copies a task with one field replaced. In load_planner, loop over every course and every task and replace task["tags"] with set(task["tags"]).

Show solution

sorted() turns a set into a list and puts the tags in a fixed order, so saving the same planner twice gives an identical file. The half-written file also shows why the safe save from the Notes builds the whole text with json.dumps first: if that fails, nothing has touched the disk yet.

#Exercise 5: An expense tracker that remembers

Write four functions: load_expenses(path) (an empty list if the file is missing), save_expenses(path, expenses) (through a .tmp file), add_expense(path, item, amount, category), which loads, appends, saves, and returns how many expenses there are now, and totals_by_category(path), which returns a dict of category totals, biggest first.

Expected output, starting from no file:

Need a hint?

add_expense doesn't keep the list in a variable between calls. Each call loads from the file, so it always sees what earlier calls saved. That's what makes it work across separate runs of the program, too. For the totals, count into a dict with .get(category, 0), then sort its items by -total.

Show solution

dict(sorted(...)) builds a new dictionary from the sorted pairs. Dictionaries keep the order their keys were added in, so the biggest category prints first.

#Exercise 6: One file per month

Write save_month(folder, month, expenses), which creates the folder if needed and saves the list as <month>.json inside it, and yearly_report(folder), which finds every .json file in the folder, in order, and returns a report string with each month's count and total plus a grand total.

Test it by saving three months out of order: 2026-10 with a 6.50 lunch and a 12.00 book, 2026-09 with a 20.00 bus pass, and 2026-11 with no expenses at all. Then print(yearly_report("months")) should show:

Need a hint?

Path(folder).glob("*.json") finds every file ending in .json in that folder, in no guaranteed order, so wrap it in sorted(). Year-month names like 2026-09 sort correctly as text. path.stem is the file name without .json.

Show solution

Keeping the months in their own folder matters: glob("*.json") in your main project folder would also pick up questions.json, scores.json, and anything else that happens to end in .json.

#Challenge: Give the contacts manager a memory

Make Module 3's contacts manager keep its contacts in contacts.json beside the script. Write load_contacts(path), returning (contacts, warning), and save_contacts(path, contacts). Your loader must handle four situations:

  1. No file yet: an empty list and no warning.
  2. A damaged file: rename it to contacts.json.bak, return an empty list and a warning.
  3. Valid JSON that isn't a list: an empty list and a warning.
  4. A list where some records are missing a name, phone, or email: keep the good ones and say how many were skipped.

Then change main() to load at the start and save after every successful add and delete. Test the loader by simulating several sessions in one script.

Need a hint?

Write a small is_contact(record) that checks the record is a dict and that name, phone, and email are all strings; all(...) with a generator does the "all three" part in one line. Save immediately after each change rather than when the user quits, so a crash or a closed terminal can't lose anything the user already entered.

Each "session" calls load_contacts fresh, just as a new run of the program would, and finds exactly what the previous one saved. Notice the order of the checks in the loader: it can't ask whether the data is a list until it knows the file exists and parses. m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Use import, from … import, and as, and explain where Python looks for a module.
  • Reach for random, datetime, and collections instead of writing that code yourself.
  • Split code into your own module and protect test code with if __name__ == "__main__":.
  • Record a project's packages in requirements.txt so it runs on another computer.
  • Catch a ValueError with try/except and re-prompt until the input is valid.

Maya wrote focus.py, a study timer that downloads a quote of the day and then asks how many minutes to focus. It works every time on her laptop. She sends it to Jordan, and it dies before printing a single word:

Jordan installs the missing package and tries again. At the prompt Minutes to focus: he types twenty, and the program crashes with a ValueError. When he types -5, it cheerfully starts a timer for negative five minutes. These look like three separate bugs, but they share one cause: the script assumed things about the computer and about the person typing, and never checked any of them. This lesson fixes both halves.

#What import does, and where Python looks

A module is a file of Python code that other code can use. import random finds a file called random.py, runs it once, and hands you a name, random, that holds everything the file defined. You then reach inside with a dot: random.randint(1, 6).

There are three ways to write an import, and you'll see all of them in real projects:

from datetime import date lets you write date(...) instead of datetime.date(...). That's shorter, but the reader can no longer see where date came from, so keep from imports to names you use a lot. random.seed(7) makes the "random" numbers repeat the same way every run, which is handy when you're testing. Delete the seed line and the die roll will change each time.

When you write import tasks, Python searches a list of folders in order and stops at the first match:

Your own folder comes first. That's what lets you import your own files, and it's also the source of one of the most confusing bugs in Python (see the warning further down).

#The standard library already wrote it for you

Python ships with a few hundred modules, called the standard library, and they're already installed wherever Python is. Before you write a helper, spend a minute checking whether it exists. Three modules show up in almost every project in this course.

#random: choices, shuffles, and dice

choice picks one item, sample picks k different items (here all four, which gives a shuffled copy), and randint(1, 6) includes both ends, unlike range.

#datetime: real calendar math

Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta, and .days turns it into a plain number. Months have different lengths and leap years exist, so counting days by hand goes wrong in ways you won't notice until February. fromisoformat reads the YYYY-MM-DD format, which is also the safest way to store dates in a JSON file.

#collections: counting and grouping

Counter does the "make a dictionary of counts" loop in one call. A defaultdict(list) creates an empty list the first time you use a new key, so you never have to write if subject not in by_subject: again.

#Your own file is a module too

Any .py file in the same folder can be imported by its name, without the .py. Say you keep a helper that formats minutes:

The stray Testing: line appears because importing a module runs it, top to bottom. Every Python file gets a variable called __name__. When you run the file directly, it's set to "__main__". When another file imports it, it's set to the module's name, "units". So you can fence off code that should only run when the file is the one you started:

Now python units.py still prints the test, and python planner.py prints only Study time this week: 4h 10m.

#Why it runs on Maya's laptop and not Jordan's

requests isn't in the standard library. It's a third-party package that Maya installed months ago with pip and forgot about. Nothing in her script says it needs it. The fix is to write the dependency down in a file called requirements.txt that travels with the code:

Running pip as python -m pip guarantees the package lands in the same Python that will run your script, which avoids the "I installed it but it still says not found" problem when a computer has two Pythons. On macOS and Linux the command is often python3 instead of python.

The .venv virtual environment from Module 1 is the other half of the fix. Packages installed while it's active belong to that project alone, so requirements.txt lists exactly what the project uses, not everything you've ever installed. When Jordan opens the folder, Python: Create Environment in the Command Palette builds his own .venv and offers to install from requirements.txt in the same step. "It works on my machine" becomes "it works on any machine that runs the install command."

📝 Note

Hard-coded paths break shared scripts too. open("C:/Users/maya/Desktop/tasks.json") fails on every computer except Maya's. Use a path relative to the project folder, like open("tasks.json"), and run the script from that folder.

#Validate input: catch the crash, check the range, ask again

input() always returns a string. int("twenty") can't turn that into a number, so it raises a ValueError, and an exception nobody handles ends the program:

try/except lets you handle it instead. Python runs the try block. If a ValueError happens anywhere inside it, Python jumps straight to the except block rather than crashing:

Catching the crash is only half the job. -5 is a perfectly good integer, so int() accepts it; you have to check the range yourself. Put both checks in a loop that only exits with a good value, and wrap it in a function so every prompt in your program can use it:

continue skips the rest of the loop body and asks again. return is the only way out, so the line after ask_int(...) can trust minutes completely. Step through it and watch text and number on each pass:

The try block holds only the one line that can fail. If you put the range check inside it too, a bug in that code could be mistaken for "the user typed letters."

⚠️ Watch out

Naming your file after a module. Save a practice file as random.py and import random finds your file first, because your folder is searched before the standard library. Python 3.13 spells it out:

AttributeError: module 'random' has no attribute 'randint' (consider renaming '…/random.py' since it has the same name as the standard library module named 'random' and the import system gives it precedence)

Rename the file (dice_game.py) and run again. Watch for random.py, math.py, json.py, and statistics.py.

⚠️ Watch out

A bare except: hides everything. except: with no exception name catches every error, including a typo like numbr (a NameError) and even Ctrl+C, so a re-prompt loop with a bare except can't be stopped from the keyboard. Name the error you expect: except ValueError:.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You save a file as random.py containing import random and print(random.randint(1, 6)). What happens when you run it?

  • It would, if Python found the standard library first. Your own folder is searched first.

  • Your file is the first random.py on the search path, and it doesn't define randint.

  • The module is found; it's just the wrong one.

Show answer

B. Your file is the first random.py on the search path, and it doesn't define randint.

2ask_int("Pick 1-10: ", 1, 10) gets the inputs 4.5, 12, 7. What does it return, and how many times does it prompt?

  • int("4.5") doesn't round; it raises ValueError.

  • 12 is a valid integer but fails the range check, so the loop asks again.

  • 4.5 fails int(), 12 fails the range check, and 7 passes both.

Show answer

C. 4.5 fails int(), 12 fails the range check, and 7 passes both.

3helpers.py ends with if __name__ == "__main__": run_tests(). What happens to run_tests() when main.py does import helpers?

  • The guard is only true for the file you started with python.

  • That's what happens with no guard at all.

  • Every file can have the guard; only the started file sees "__main__".

Show answer

A. The guard is only true for the file you started with python.

4Jordan gets ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests' running Maya's project. What's the right fix?

  • Fragile, and it skips the packages requests itself depends on.

  • The file lists what the project needs, so one command installs it anywhere.

  • There's no such module; renaming imports doesn't install anything.

Show answer

B. The file lists what the project needs, so one command installs it anywhere.

Key takeaways

  • import x runs x.py once and gives you the name x; from x import y gives you just y.
  • Python searches your script's folder first, so never name a file after a module you use.
  • Check the standard library (random, datetime, collections, …) before writing a helper.
  • Use if __name__ == "__main__": for code that should run only when the file is started directly.
  • List third-party packages in requirements.txt and install them into a virtual environment.
  • Validate in two steps, conversion (try/except ValueError) and range, inside a loop that only returns good values.

What you'll learn

  • Generate repeatable random questions with random.Random(seed).
  • Reuse a validated ask_int() loop and move it into its own module.
  • Add command-line options with argparse, including type=int and defaults.
  • Check option values that argparse can't check for you, using parser.error().
  • Summarize mistakes with collections.Counter.

Typing practice into a terminal is faster than flash cards, and a program can notice patterns you can't, like the fact that every question you miss has a 9 in it. Here's the finished drill running in the VS Code terminal. The learner typed the numbers after each =, plus one typo:

Notice three design decisions already. The typo eighty one gets a second chance instead of counting as wrong. --count and --seed are options on the command line, not questions the program asks. And the summary turns a list of misses into advice.

Make a folder called drill and open it in VS Code. Every cell below runs for real, and later cells use the functions from earlier ones, the same way your file grows as you add to it.

#Step 1: Make one random question

random.Random(11) creates a random-number generator of our own, started from the seed 11. Two generators with the same seed produce the same numbers in the same order, which is how the session above can be repeated exactly. Passing rng into the function, instead of calling random.randint inside it, means the caller decides whether the questions are repeatable. Factors start at 2 because nobody needs to practice 1 x 7.

#Step 2: Ask until you get a number

This is the validation loop from the notes, trimmed to what a drill needs: any whole number is a valid answer, even a wrong one, so there's no range check.

.strip() removes spaces around the input, so " 81 " counts. The return sits inside the try because int(text) is the only thing that can fail: if it works, the function ends right there.

#Step 3: Run a round and remember the misses

The function returns the misses instead of printing a final report. That keeps it useful: the caller can print a score, save the misses to a file, or test the result, and run_drill doesn't need to change for any of them. Each miss is a tuple (a, b) because the pair belongs together and never changes.

#Step 4: Find the weak spots with Counter

A list like [(9, 9), (10, 9), (7, 9)] hides the pattern. Counting every factor that appears in a miss makes it obvious:

A Counter starts every key at 0, so factors[a] += 1 works the first time a number appears. most_common(2) sorts by count and returns (factor, count) pairs; the list comprehension keeps just the factors. Missing 9 x 9 counts the 9 once, since it's one mistake. An empty list of misses gives an empty answer instead of an error, and Step 6 relies on that.

#Step 5: Take options from the command line

Asking "How many questions?" every time gets old. Options typed after the file name are faster, and argparse turns them into variables:

When a real user runs the file, parse_args() reads what they typed. Here we pass a list of words instead, standing in for python drill.py --count 5 --seed 11, so we can see the result. Look at what argparse did: "5" became the integer 5 because of type=int, --up-to fell back to its default, and the dash in --up-to became an underscore in args.up_to, because a dash isn't allowed in a Python name.

You also get a help screen without writing one:

And argparse rejects bad types before your code ever sees them:

#Step 6: Check what argparse can't, and write main()

type=int happily accepts --count 0 or --up-to 5000. A zero-question drill is pointless, and factors up to 5000 aren't a times table. parser.error() prints the usage line plus your message and stops the program, so out-of-range options look exactly like the built-in errors:

That's the session from the top of the page, produced by the real code. main(argv=None) passes None to parse_args when the file runs normally, which tells argparse to read the real command line. In a test, you pass a list. When --seed is left out, args.seed is None, and random.Random(None) seeds itself from the system, so every round is different.

#Step 7: Move ask_int into its own module

ask_int has nothing to do with multiplication. Your next project will need it too, so give it a file of its own, prompts.py, in the same folder:

In drill.py, delete the ask_int definition and import it instead with from prompts import ask_int. Because both files sit in the same folder, Python finds prompts.py first on its search path.

#The finished program

Run it from the VS Code terminal with python drill.py, python drill.py --count 3 --up-to 9, or python drill.py -h. Imports go at the top in groups, with a blank line between them: the standard library first, then third-party packages (none here), then your own modules. That's the PEP 8 style most Python projects follow.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does run_drill take an rng argument instead of calling random.randint directly?

  • That's what makes --seed work, and it makes the function testable.

  • It works anywhere; the choice is about who controls the randomness.

  • Speed isn't the reason; repeatability is.

Show answer

A. That's what makes --seed work, and it makes the function testable.

2A user runs python drill.py --count 500. What happens?

  • 500 is a valid int, so type=int accepts it.

  • The range check in main() catches what type=int can't.

  • It would, without the range check.

Show answer

B. The range check in main() catches what type=int can't.

3Typing eighty one doesn't count as a wrong answer. Which part of the code makes that true?

  • That check only runs once ask_int has returned a number.

  • Validation happens before scoring, so a typo can't be scored at all.

  • argparse only handles the command line, not answers typed during the drill.

Show answer

B. Validation happens before scoring, so a typo can't be scored at all.

Key takeaways

  • Pass a random.Random(seed) into functions that need randomness so you can repeat a run.
  • Validate input where it enters the program, so the rest of the code works only with good values.
  • argparse handles types, defaults, and help; range rules still need your own parser.error() checks.
  • main(argv=None) reads the real command line normally and accepts a list when you're testing.
  • Helpers that aren't about this one program belong in their own module.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add --op with choices=["x", "+"] so the drill can practice addition too.
  • Time each round with datetime.now() before and after run_drill, and print the seconds taken.
  • Ask each missed question once more at the end, using the list run_drill returns.
  • Save each round's score and date to a JSON file and print your best score so far.

#Further reading

  • Argparse Tutorial (opens in a new tab): the official step-by-step guide, from one positional argument up to option groups.
  • random: Generate pseudo-random numbers (opens in a new tab): every function in the module, plus why seeded generators repeat.
  • collections.Counter (opens in a new tab): most_common, adding counters together, and other tricks.

What you'll learn

  • Choose the right standard library tool for a small problem.
  • Do date arithmetic with date.fromisoformat and timedelta.
  • Write validators that re-prompt for yes/no answers, dates, and menu choices.
  • Give an argparse option a custom type with a clear error message.

Each exercise has a hint and a full solution. Try for at least ten minutes before opening the solution, and type the code yourself in VS Code rather than pasting it: the typos you make and fix are part of the practice.

#Warm-up: which line fails?

Predict what this prints before you look at the output. One line crashes. Which one, and what kind of error is it?

import math gives you the name math, and from math import sqrt gives you sqrt. Nothing gave you a bare floor, so the last line is a NameError. Fix it with math.floor, or add floor to the from line.

#Exercise 1: Split the class into random teams

You have eight names. Split them into two teams of four at random, print each team in alphabetical order, and make the split repeatable with a seed so you can show a friend the same result. Don't change the original list.

Need a hint?

Copy the list with names[:], then shuffle the copy with a random.Random(4) generator. The first half of the shuffled list is Team A.

Show solution

shuffle rearranges a list in place and returns None, which is why we shuffle a copy. Writing shuffled = names would not copy anything; both names would point to the same list, and the original order would be lost. Using len(shuffled) // 2 instead of 4 keeps it working for a class of ten.

#Exercise 2: "Tomorrow", not "in 1 days"

Write days_until(deadline_text, today). It takes a date string like "2026-12-04" and a date, and returns "today", "tomorrow", "in 19 days", "yesterday", or "3 days ago". Test it with today = date(2026, 11, 15).

Need a hint?

Subtract today from the parsed deadline and take .days. That number is negative for past dates. Handle 0, 1, and -1 first, then the general cases.

Show solution

Taking today as a parameter, instead of calling date.today() inside, is what makes the output above repeatable. Your real program passes date.today(), and your tests pass a fixed date.

#Exercise 3: A yes/no question that accepts real answers

Write ask_yes_no(prompt). It should accept y, yes, n, or no in any capitalization, with or without spaces around them, and return True or False. Anything else gets a short message and the question again.

Need a hint?

Clean the answer once with .strip().lower(), then check membership with in against a set of accepted words.

Show solution

No try is needed here, because nothing raises an error: a string comparison just returns False. Use try/except when a conversion like int() can fail, and plain if checks when you only need to compare.

#Exercise 4: Ask for a due date that's real and not in the past

Write ask_date(prompt, today). Keep asking until the user types a valid YYYY-MM-DD date that is today or later. Show the reason for each rejection.

Need a hint?

except ValueError as error: gives you the exception object, and print(error) shows Python's own explanation. The "already passed" check is a plain if after the conversion succeeds.

Show solution

fromisoformat checks the calendar for you, which is why February 30 fails with its own message. Dates compare with < the way numbers do, so the past-date check is one line.

#Exercise 5: Where did the study time go?

Given this list of study sessions, print the total minutes per subject (largest first) and the subject you studied most often.

Need a hint?

A defaultdict(int) adds up minutes without checking whether the key exists. A Counter of just the subject names answers "most often." sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True) sorts by the minutes.

Show solution

"Most minutes" and "most sessions" are different questions, and here they even have the same answer by coincidence. Change history to 90 minutes and the first line changes while the last one doesn't.

#Exercise 6: A countdown command with a friendly date error

Write countdown.py that runs like python countdown.py 2026-12-18 --label "winter break" and prints 33 days until winter break. (when today is November 15). The date is a positional argument. A bad date should produce a clear message, not a traceback:

Need a hint?

type= can be any function that takes a string. Write iso_date(text) that calls date.fromisoformat and, on ValueError, raises argparse.ArgumentTypeError with your message. argparse prints that message for you.

Show solution

In the real file, end with if __name__ == "__main__": main() so it reads the real command line and today's date. Positional arguments have no dashes and are required, so python countdown.py alone prints "the following arguments are required: deadline".

#Challenge: A study-log menu that can't be broken

Build a menu loop with three choices: a adds a study session (1 to 240 minutes), s shows the number of sessions and total minutes, and q quits. Bad menu letters, non-numbers, and out-of-range minutes all get a message and another try. Nothing the user types should crash it.

Need a hint?

Write two small helpers first, ask_choice(prompt, options) and ask_int(prompt, low, high), and test each one alone. Then the menu loop is just if/elif on a choice you already know is valid.

Show solution

The menu code never checks for bad input itself. Each helper promises to return only valid values, so the loop body can be short and trusting. That split, where input is checked at the door and logic assumes it's clean, is the same one you'll use in every project for the rest of the course.

What you'll learn

  • Follow a repeatable debugging loop: reproduce, gather evidence, test one idea, fix, confirm.
  • Read a traceback from the bottom up and find the line that matters.
  • Use print(f"{name=}") and repr to see values exactly, quotes and spaces included.
  • Add assert checks that stop the program the moment its data goes wrong.
  • Replace debug prints with logging, so they can be turned off without deleting them.
  • Shrink a bug into a minimal reproduction.

The supply-room program has one job: when a delivery of 30 pens arrives, add 30 to the pen count. Erasers work fine. Pens don't change at all. Pencils, which nobody touched, jump from 40 to 70:

You could start changing lines and rerunning until the numbers look right. That sometimes works, and when it does you've learned nothing and may have added a second bug. A better approach treats a bug like an experiment: collect evidence, form one guess, and test exactly that guess.

#The debugging loop

Apply it to the supply room. Reproduce: restocking "eraser" works and "pen" doesn't, every time. Evidence: the pen's extra 30 landed on the pencil, so find_item("pen") probably returned the wrong dictionary. Test that one idea: step through find_item("pen") and watch which item it stops on.

It returns on the very first pass. "pen" in "pencil" asks whether "pen" appears anywhere inside "pencil", and it does. Erasers worked only because no earlier item contains the letters "eraser". The fix is if item["name"] == name:, and the confirm step means rerunning both the pen and the eraser cases, not just the one that was broken.

#Read a traceback from the bottom up

When a program crashes, Python prints a traceback: the chain of function calls that was running at the moment of the crash. It looks scary because it's long, but you read it in a fixed order.

  1. The last line is the error type and message: KeyError: 'price'. A KeyError means a dictionary didn't have the key you asked for, and the message names the key.
  2. The frame just above it is where it happened: line 4, inside total_value, on item["qty"] * item["price"].
  3. Frames further up are who called whom. Read upward when you need to know how the program got there: the module called report, which called total_value.

The crash is on line 4, but line 4 is fine. The real mistake is in the data: the pen's dictionary says "cost" instead of "price". The line that crashes is where the problem was noticed, which isn't always where it was made. Also notice that Items: 2 printed before the crash, which proves report started and got halfway.

💡 Tip

In a long traceback from a library, skip frames from files you didn't write (paths containing site-packages or the Python install folder). The lowest frame that points at your file is usually the place to start.

#Print the truth, not a look-alike

A plain print can hide exactly what you need to see. Strings print without quotes, so a trailing space vanishes, and the string "12" looks just like the number 12:

The = inside an f-string prints the expression, an equals sign, and the value's repr: the way you'd write it in code. Now the quotes show qty is text and the gap before the closing quote shows the space in name. When a lookup "can't find" something you can see on the screen, this is the first print to write.

#Make the program check itself with assert

assert condition, message says "this must be true here." If it isn't, Python stops with an AssertionError and your message:

Without the assert, the eraser would quietly sit at -4 until some report much later printed nonsense. With it, the program stops on the exact call that broke the rule. Use asserts for things that should be impossible if your code is right. Don't use them to check what a user typed: running Python with python -O removes every assert, and user mistakes need friendly messages anyway, the kind you wrote in Module 5.

#Logging: prints you can turn down

Debug prints pile up. You add six to find a bug, delete four, forget two, and now your program's output has HERE!! in it. The logging module gives each message a level (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL), and one setting decides which levels appear:

After the level changes to WARNING, the DEBUG lines disappear while the warnings keep coming. The code didn't change, only the setting. The format string adds the function name to every line for free, which is evidence you'd otherwise type by hand. (Logging normally writes to the terminal's error stream; stream=sys.stdout here keeps it in order with the print output.)

#Stuck? Explain it to a duck, then shrink it

Rubber duck debugging means explaining your code, line by line and out loud, to someone who knows nothing, even a rubber duck. It works because explaining forces you to say what each line actually does instead of what you meant: "this loop checks whether the name is in the item's name... oh."

If that doesn't crack it, build a minimal reproduction: copy the program and delete everything that isn't needed for the bug to happen. Remove the file loading, then the menu, then all but two items. Each time, rerun; if the bug vanishes, the last thing you deleted was involved. The supply-room bug shrinks to a single line:

Often you find the bug while shrinking. If you don't, you now have something small enough to show a teacher or post online, along with the full traceback, what you expected, and what happened instead.

⚠️ Watch out

Changing several things at once. If you edit three lines and the bug disappears, you don't know which edit fixed it, or whether one of the others broke something new. Change one thing, rerun, and look.

⚠️ Watch out

Fixing the symptom. Adding if name == "pen": inventory[1]["qty"] += change makes pens work and leaves "cat" matching "bobcat". If your fix mentions the exact value from the bug report, ask whether you've found the cause yet.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A traceback has five frames and ends with TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +=: 'int' and 'str'. Where do you look first?

  • The top frame is usually just the line that called main(); it rarely contains the bug.

  • The last line says what went wrong, and the lowest frame in your code says where.

  • The paths are unique to your computer; the error line is what to search for.

Show answer

B. The last line says what went wrong, and the lowest frame in your code says where.

2print(f"{qty=}") prints qty='12'. What have you learned?

  • The quotes say otherwise.

  • The repr shows quotes around text, so '12' is a string, not the number 12.

  • A trailing space would show as '12 ' inside the quotes.

Show answer

B. The repr shows quotes around text, so '12' is a string, not the number 12.

3Which is the best place for an assert?

  • Asserts vanish under python -O and give users a crash instead of help.

  • That's a rule your own code must never break, so a crash pinpoints the bug.

  • Asserts work when they state specific rules, not as a general safety net.

Show answer

B. That's a rule your own code must never break, so a crash pinpoints the bug.

4You shrink a 200-line program to 6 lines that still show the bug. What's the main benefit?

  • Speed isn't the point.

  • Every line you deleted without fixing the bug was ruled out as the cause.

  • The traceback format is the same at any length.

Show answer

B. Every line you deleted without fixing the bug was ruled out as the cause.

Key takeaways

  • Debug like an experiment: reproduce it, gather evidence, test one hypothesis, fix, then confirm.
  • Read tracebacks bottom up: the error line, then the lowest frame in your own code.
  • The crashing line is where a problem was noticed, not always where it was made.
  • print(f"{x=}") shows the repr, so quotes, spaces, and types become visible.
  • assert turns a silent bad state into an immediate, labeled stop.
  • logging levels let you keep debug messages in the code and hide them with one setting.
  • When stuck, explain it aloud, then shrink it to a minimal reproduction.

#Further reading

  • Logging HOWTO (opens in a new tab): the official guide; the basic tutorial at the top covers everything in this lesson.
  • Deciphering Python's Traceback (opens in a new tab): Trey Hunner's short article on reading tracebacks bottom up, with a narrated version.
  • How to create a Minimal, Reproducible Example (opens in a new tab): Stack Overflow's guide to asking for help with code people can actually run.

What you'll learn

  • Reproduce a bug and write down expected versus actual results before touching the code.
  • Set breakpoints and start the Python Debugger in VS Code.
  • Step through a loop with Continue and Step Over while reading the Variables and Watch panes.
  • Use a conditional breakpoint and the Debug Console to test one hypothesis.
  • Fix the bug and add a regression check so it can't quietly come back.

The school store's bug report: "At the end of the day, the program should remove everything that sold out. Monday it worked. Tuesday, tape sold out and it's still on the list with 0 left." Same code, different days, different results. Staring won't find this one; a debugger will.

By the end of this build, the fixed program and its check will print this:

#Step 1: Reproduce it, and write down what you expected

Create store.py in your project folder and paste this in. It runs both days from the report:

Now write the evidence down, in a comment or on paper:

Day Sold out Expected Actual
Monday glue pencil, tape, ruler pencil, tape, ruler
Tuesday glue, tape pencil, ruler pencil, tape 0, ruler

The bug happens every time we run Tuesday, and the table holds a clue: it only goes wrong when two items sell out. Tape is at 0, so apply_sales did its job. The suspect is remove_sold_out.

#Step 2: Pause the program with a breakpoint

A breakpoint tells the debugger "stop just before running this line, and let me look around."

  1. Move your mouse to the left of the line number for if item["qty"] == 0:. A faint red dot appears in the margin; click it. The dot stays, solid red. (Pressing F9 with the cursor on the line does the same.)
  2. Click the small down arrow next to the Run triangle at the top right of the editor and choose Python Debugger: Debug Python File. If VS Code instead asks you to pick a debugger or configuration, choose Python Debugger, then Python File.
  3. The program runs until it reaches your line, then freezes. The line is highlighted, the Run and Debug view opens on the left, and a small toolbar appears at the top of the window.

The Run and Debug view has four sections: VARIABLES (everything that exists right now), WATCH (expressions you choose), CALL STACK (which function called which, like a live traceback), and BREAKPOINTS. Under VARIABLES, expand Locals, then item: it's {'name': 'pencil', 'qty': 35}.

📝 Note

Monday's run reaches the breakpoint first, because it runs first. From the first pause, press F5 (Continue) three times to get through Monday, and the next pause is Tuesday's first item. Jot down which items Monday stops on; you'll want them in a minute.

#Step 3: Step through the loop and watch the list

The toolbar buttons are the debugger's controls. These are the Windows and Linux shortcuts; on a Mac some function keys need the Fn key held down.

Button Key What it does
Continue F5 run until the next breakpoint
Step Over F10 run the current line, then pause on the next one
Step Into F11 go inside the function this line calls
Step Out Shift+F11 finish this function and pause in the caller
Restart Ctrl+Shift+F5 start the run again
Stop Shift+F5 end the debug session

Make the list itself visible. In the WATCH section, click + and type [i["name"] for i in inventory], then press Enter. A watch expression is re-evaluated every time the program pauses.

Now, paused at Tuesday's first item, press F5 repeatedly and note item["name"] at each stop: pencil, glue, ruler, then the program ends. Four items, three visits. Monday's stops were the same three, so Monday skipped tape too; it did no harm because tape wasn't sold out. That's why the bug seemed to happen only sometimes: the skip happens whenever an item is removed, but it only shows when the skipped item also needed removing.

You can replay the same thing here, one line at a time; watch item and the list's length:

The loop never says checking tape. That's the key piece of evidence: tape wasn't checked and rejected, it was never checked at all.

#Step 4: Stop only when it matters

With 400 items, pressing F5 hundreds of times is miserable. A conditional breakpoint pauses only when an expression is true. Click the red dot to remove your breakpoint. Then right-click in the margin next to the same if line, choose Add Conditional Breakpoint, leave the type as Expression, type item["name"] == "tape", and press Enter. The dot changes shape to show it has a condition.

Start the debugger again. It never pauses. The condition is checked every time the line runs, so never pausing proves item was never tape on that line. "I think it skips tape" is now a fact.

💡 Tip

Right-click the margin and choose Add Logpoint to print a message without editing your code. A logpoint like checking {item["name"]} writes to the Debug Console every time the line runs and never pauses. It's a print you can't forget to delete.

#Step 5: Test the hypothesis in the Debug Console

Here's a hypothesis: removing an item shifts everything after it one place to the left, and the for loop, which counts positions, steps past whatever slid into the gap. Test it directly.

Remove the conditional breakpoint and put a plain one on the inventory.remove(item) line. Start debugging and continue until item is glue on Tuesday. Open the Debug Console (View → Debug Console, or Ctrl+Shift+Y) and type expressions at the > prompt. They run inside the paused program:

Press F10 once to run the remove line, then ask again:

Tape slid from position 2 into position 1. The loop has already done position 1, so its next pass looks at position 2, which is now ruler. Hypothesis confirmed, with evidence. Press Shift+F5 to stop.

#Step 6: Shrink it to four lines

Before fixing, prove you understand the cause by reproducing it with no inventory, no dictionaries, and no sales:

The second 0 survives for the same reason tape did. Now the bug has nothing to do with stores, and the rule is clear: don't add to or remove from a list while a for loop is walking through it.

#Step 7: Fix it and lock it in

The fix is to stop removing and instead build a new list of the items to keep. A list comprehension reads the old list without changing it:

The first check is the bug report's exact situation, two sold-out items in a row, shrunk to the smallest data that shows it. That's a regression check: a test for a bug you already fixed, so if someone "simplifies" the function back to a remove loop, it fails right away. The other two cover edges: everything sold out, and an empty store. If the first assert fails, its second part prints what the function really returned.

#The finished program

remove_sold_out is gone. end_of_day now replaces its list with the filtered one, and the check runs first:

Tuesday is right, and Monday is unchanged. Rechecking the case that already worked is the "confirm" step people skip.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1In Step 4, the conditional breakpoint item["name"] == "tape" never paused. Why is that useful evidence?

  • It was set up correctly; the debugger checks the condition every time the line runs.

  • A condition that's never true across every run of the line rules out "tape was checked and kept."

  • The watch already showed tape at 0; the breakpoint is about whether the loop visited it.

Show answer

B. A condition that's never true across every run of the line rules out "tape was checked and kept."

2Why does the fix build a new list instead of removing items one at a time more carefully?

  • The loop's position counter can't get out of step with a list that doesn't change.

  • A for loop that appends to a new list works too; the point is not mutating the list being looped over.

  • remove worked fine; the problem was when it ran.

Show answer

A. The loop's position counter can't get out of step with a list that doesn't change.

3The check uses two sold-out items in a row as its first test. Why that case?

  • An empty list is shorter, and there's a separate check for it.

  • A regression check recreates the bug's conditions in the smallest form.

  • Asserts work with any expression that's true or false.

Show answer

B. A regression check recreates the bug's conditions in the smallest form.

Key takeaways

  • Write down expected versus actual first; the pattern in that table often points at the suspect.
  • A breakpoint pauses before its line runs, and the Variables pane shows the program's state at that moment.
  • Watch expressions and the Debug Console let you ask your own questions of the paused program.
  • A conditional breakpoint that never fires is evidence too: that state never happened on that line.
  • Don't add to or remove from a list inside a for loop over that same list; build a new one.
  • Turn every fixed bug into a regression check that uses the bug's exact conditions.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a breakpoint inside apply_sales and use Step Into from end_of_day to watch a sale happen.
  • Make apply_sales raise a ValueError for a name that isn't in the inventory, and add a check for it.
  • Add a check that apply_sales never makes a quantity negative, then find a sale that breaks it.

#Further reading

  • Python debugging in VS Code (opens in a new tab): starting the Python Debugger, and passing command-line arguments through launch.json.
  • Debug code with Visual Studio Code (opens in a new tab): every pane, breakpoint type, and toolbar button, for any language.
  • The Python Tutorial: for statements (opens in a new tab): the official note on why changing a collection while looping over it is tricky, with the safer patterns.

What you'll learn

  • Locate a crash from its traceback and decide where the fix belongs.
  • Find silent bugs (wrong output, no crash) with targeted print(f"{x=}") evidence.
  • Swap debug prints for logging and control them with a level.
  • Use a conditional breakpoint or an assert to find the first moment data goes wrong.
  • Recognize two shared-object bugs: the mutable default argument and the shallow copy.

Every exercise here contains a real bug. Before you open a hint, write one sentence: "I think the bug is ___ because ___." Then gather evidence for or against it. Being wrong is fine; guessing without testing is the habit to break.

#Warm-up: what does each print show?

Predict both lines before you look.

The first print hides a newline: 3.0 lands on the next line and nothing says why. It also doesn't tell you whether 3.0 is a number or text. The second shows 'Yes\n', so answer == "Yes" would be False, and it confirms count is a float. Two bugs found before reading any other code.

#Exercise 1: The report that crashes in the middle

Read the traceback and answer three questions before fixing anything: which line raised the error, which piece of data caused it, and where the fix should go. Then make Period 2 print Period 2: no scores yet while the other periods still print their averages.

Need a hint?

The lowest frame is inside average, but average has no way to print "no scores yet". Which function knows the period's name?

Show solution

The error is raised on line 2 (sum(scores) / len(scores)), the data is Period 2's empty list, and Period 1: 85.0 printed first, which proves the loop got one period in. Dividing by len([]) is dividing by zero.

average reports "there's no answer" by returning None, and class_report, which knows the name, decides what to print. The crash happened in one function, and the fix touched both.

#Exercise 2: The best score that isn't

best_score([97, 85, 90]) should return 97. It returns 90, and there's no error. Add one debug print inside the loop that shows which index and value it checks on each pass, read the evidence, then fix it.

Need a hint?

Print f"{i=} {scores[i]=} {best=}" as the first line of the loop. How many passes do you see, and which index is missing?

Show solution

Only two passes, and index 0, the 97, is never checked. range(1, len(scores)) starts at 1. The clean fix loops over the values directly, so there's no index to get wrong:

Starting best at scores[0] instead of 0 also fixes a second, hidden bug: with all-negative values, the old version would return 0, a number that isn't in the list. (In real code, max(scores) does all of this.)

#Exercise 3: "No such item," but it's right there

A user types Glue (with a capital G and a trailing space) and gets No such item. Use evidence to show exactly why, then fix it so capitalization and spaces don't matter.

Need a hint?

Print repr(name) or f"{name=}" right after the input line. Then compare it with the keys of stock.

Show solution

raw='Glue ' shows both problems at once: the capital G and the space. Dictionary keys must match exactly, so clean the input once, right where it enters the program. Delete the two debug prints when you're done.

#Exercise 4: From print spam to logging

This function prints details on every call, and the output is drowning the useful line. Convert it to logging: the details become DEBUG messages, the low-stock alert becomes a WARNING, and the final summary stays a normal print. Run it once at DEBUG level and once at WARNING level.

Need a hint?

Call logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s") once at the top. To switch levels later in the same program, use logging.getLogger().setLevel(logging.WARNING).

Show solution

At WARNING, only the alerts remain, and the debug lines are still in the code for the next time you need them. stream=sys.stdout is only there so the log lines appear in order with the prints on this page; in your own terminal you can leave it out.

#Exercise 5: Every new task has everyone's tags

Each new task should start with only the tag "new". Instead, the tags pile up across tasks. Prove that the tasks are sharing one list, write a minimal reproduction of the cause, and fix it.

Need a hint?

a["tags"] is b["tags"] asks whether two names point to the same list object, not just equal ones. When is the default [] created: each call, or once?

Show solution

True proves it: there is one list, shared by every call that relies on the default. Python evaluates tags=[] once, when the def line runs, not each time the function is called. The standard fix uses None as the default and makes a fresh list inside:

tags + ["new"] builds a new list, so even a list the caller passed in isn't changed behind their back.

#Exercise 6: When did glue go negative?

This simulation runs 300 orders, and the month-end report shows glue at -15. A shelf can't hold negative glue, so some order took more than was there. Find the first order where glue went below zero, and what that order was.

Need a hint?

In VS Code, right-click the margin next to stock[name] += change, choose Add Conditional Breakpoint, and use the expression stock[name] + change < 0. Debug the file, and when it pauses, read number, name, change, and stock in the Variables pane. No debugger handy? An assert after the update finds the same moment.

Show solution

The debugger pauses once, with number = 104, name = 'glue', change = -2, and glue at 1. Here's the same answer found with an assert, which states the rule and stops the instant it breaks:

Without this, you'd see only the final -15 and have no idea when it started. The real fix belongs in the code that takes orders: reject or shorten any sale bigger than what's on the shelf.

#Challenge: The undo button that doesn't undo

The program saves a snapshot before each change so the user can undo. After a sale and an undo, the pen count should be back to 12. It's 7. Find out why with evidence, try dict(inventory) as a fix and explain why it still fails, then fix it for real.

Need a hint?

Print history[0] is inventory right after saving the snapshot. Then try history.append(dict(inventory)) and print history[0]["pen"] is inventory["pen"]. The copy module has a function that copies all the way down.

Show solution

history.append(inventory) doesn't copy anything; it stores a second reference to the same dictionary, so the "snapshot" changes along with the original. dict(inventory) makes a new outer dictionary, but its values are the same inner dictionaries (that's the diagram above), and the sale changes an inner one. copy.deepcopy copies every level, so the snapshot is truly separate. This is the same family of bug as Exercise 5: two names, one object, and a change through one name that shows up through the other.

What you'll learn

  • Write a tool's commands and data shape before writing its code.
  • Separate a program into interface, logic, and storage, and say what belongs in each.
  • Build argparse subcommands and send each one to its own handler function.
  • Give a program one entry point, main(argv=None), that returns an exit code.
  • List what a useful README contains.

Sam's homework planner started as one function. Now planner.py has fourteen of them, and the only way to use it is to scroll to the bottom, uncomment the call you want, and press Run. Here's one of the fourteen:

Nothing in it is wrong, exactly. But it asks a question, reads a file, changes data, writes a file, and prints, all at once. You can't test it without typing at a prompt and owning a real tasks.json. You can't call it from a command like python planner.py add "Lab report". And if the file doesn't exist yet, it crashes. The code isn't the problem; the missing design is.

#Start from what the user types

Before any code, write down exactly how someone will use the tool, as if you were writing its instruction card:

Then write down the data that has to survive between runs:

These two sketches answer most design questions early. Tasks need an id, because typing done 2 is easier than retyping a title. Dates are strings in YYYY-MM-DD form, because JSON has no date type. list hides finished work unless you ask for --all. If you can't write the commands and the data, you're not ready to write the program, and that's useful to discover before you've written 200 lines.

#Three layers: interface, logic, storage

Most command-line tools split cleanly into three jobs. Keeping them in separate functions, and later separate files, is the single biggest step from "script" to "project."

Layer Its job Never does
Interface read the command line, print results and errors the actual calculations
Logic change and query the data, raise ValueError for bad requests print, input, or open files
Storage turn the file into Python data and back decide what the data means

The logic layer is the heart, and its rule is strict: it takes data in and hands data back. That makes it testable with nothing but assert:

No prompt, no file, no printing inside add_task, and yet it does all the real work, including the rule that blank titles aren't allowed. It raises an error rather than printing one, because only the interface knows whether that error should go to a terminal, a test, or someday a web page. max(..., default=0) handles the empty list, so the first task gets id 1.

#Subcommands: one tool, several verbs

git commit, git push, pip install: each tool has subcommands, and each subcommand has its own arguments. argparse builds this with add_subparsers:

dest="command" stores which subcommand was used, so args.command is "add", "done", or "list". Each subcommand only gets its own arguments: there's no args.id after add. action="store_true" makes --all a switch that's False unless typed. And required=True means running the tool with no subcommand prints a usage error instead of doing nothing. The help screen comes for free:

#One way in: main() and exit codes

Now connect the layers. Each subcommand gets a small handler function, and main() picks the right one with a dictionary. A dictionary of functions is cleaner than a long if args.command == ... chain, and adding a command means adding one line.

Every run returns an exit code: 0 means success and anything else means failure. Other programs, scripts, and graders read this number to know whether your tool worked. The fourth call returned 1. Its message went to sys.stderr, the error stream, which this page doesn't display but your terminal does:

(echo $? prints the last exit code on macOS and Linux; in PowerShell, use $LASTEXITCODE.) The last lines of a real plan.py connect main() to the terminal:

When you run the file, main() gets None, so argparse reads the real command line, and sys.exit passes the return value to the shell. When a test file imports plan, the guard is false and nothing runs, so the test can call main(["done", "9"]) itself and check that it returns 1.

#The README is part of the design

A README is the first file anyone opens, including you in three months. Write it while the design is fresh, and update it when commands change. A good one answers five questions:

What is it, what do I need, how do I use it (with examples you can copy), how is it organized, and what doesn't it do. The usage examples are the same ones you wrote before coding, so the README is half done before the program is.

⚠️ Watch out

Logic that prints. If add_task prints "Added!" itself, then every caller gets that message, including tests and other commands that reuse it. Return a value or raise an error, and let the interface decide what to show.

⚠️ Watch out

Code at the bottom with no guard. A bare main() on the last line runs the moment another file imports yours, so importing plan in a test starts reading the test runner's command-line arguments and fails with a confusing usage error. Always use if __name__ == "__main__":.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Where does a function that turns a task into the text [x] #1 Read chapter 4 belong?

  • Deciding how things look to the user is the interface's job.

  • Logic decides what's true about the data; formatting it for a screen is presentation.

  • Storage only converts between the file and Python data.

Show answer

A. Deciding how things look to the user is the interface's job.

2Why does main take argv=None instead of always reading the real command line?

  • parse_args() works fine with no argument at all.

  • None means "read the real command line"; a list stands in for what a user would type.

  • Speed is the same either way.

Show answer

B. None means "read the real command line"; a list stands in for what a user would type.

3After parse_args(["done", "2"]), what is args.id?

  • type=int converted it before your code saw it.

  • The done subcommand declared id with type=int.

  • id here is the argument the user typed, not the task's stored id.

Show answer

B. The done subcommand declared id with type=int.

4A grading script runs your tool and sees exit code 1. What does it conclude?

  • Exit codes don't count output.

  • 0 means success; any nonzero code means something went wrong.

  • That would be exit code 0.

Show answer

B. 0 means success; any nonzero code means something went wrong.

Key takeaways

  • Design in this order: commands and sample output, then the data shape, then code.
  • Interface reads input and prints; logic changes data and raises errors; storage reads and writes files.
  • Logic functions that return values can be tested with plain assert, no typing or files needed.
  • add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True) gives one tool several verbs, each with its own arguments.
  • A dictionary from command names to handler functions keeps main() short.
  • main(argv=None) returns an exit code; sys.exit(main()) under the __name__ guard hands it to the shell.
  • A README answers: what is it, what do I need, how do I use it, how is it organized, and what are its limits.

#Further reading

  • argparse: Sub-commands (opens in a new tab): the official reference for add_subparsers, with the full list of options.
  • __main__: Top-level code environment (opens in a new tab): how __name__ works and the recommended main() pattern.
  • Command Line Interface Guidelines (opens in a new tab): an excellent, readable guide to designing command-line tools that people enjoy using.

m7-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a list of commands and a data shape into a working multi-file tool.
  • Write a storage layer that handles a missing file and a damaged one.
  • Write logic functions that enforce the rules and raise ValueError instead of printing.
  • Connect argparse subcommands to handler functions through one main().
  • Split the code into modules and document it with a README.

You're going to build shelf.py, a reading log for the terminal. It remembers every book between runs, tracks pages, and refuses nonsense politely. Here's a real session with the finished tool:

Titles match without caring about capital letters, reading past the last page just finishes the book, and a typo gets a message that tells you what to do next. The quotes around "The Hobbit" keep a two-word title together as one argument.

Make a folder called shelf and open it in VS Code. We'll build each layer in this page first, where every cell runs, then split it into files.

#Step 1: Write the commands and the data first

The session above is the command design. The data design is one JSON list, one dictionary per book:

Store only facts, not things you can calculate. There's no "percent" or "finished" field, because both come from read and pages. If they were stored, they could disagree with the numbers they came from, and then which one is true?

#Step 2: Storage that survives a missing or damaged file

The first run of any tool has no data file, and that's normal, so FileNotFoundError becomes an empty shelf. A damaged file is not normal. Returning [] there would be a disaster: the next save_books would overwrite the user's whole reading history with an empty list. So storage turns it into a ValueError with a helpful message, which the interface will report. encoding="utf-8" keeps titles like Les Misérables safe on every operating system.

#Step 3: The rules, with no printing

find_book uses == after lowercasing both sides, never in, so "Hat" can't match "Hatchet" (that's the supply-room bug from Module 6). min(...) caps the pages read at the book's length, so logging 250 pages of a 195-page book finishes it instead of reaching 128%. And every rule raises a ValueError with a sentence a user could act on. *bad unpacks each tuple into the two arguments, so one loop tests three bad requests.

#Step 4: Handlers and the parser

Each subcommand gets a handler that takes the books and the parsed arguments and returns the message to show. Handlers translate between the terminal's world (strings, flags) and the logic's world (books, numbers).

--pages uses required=True because a book without a length can't show progress. It's still written as an option so the command reads clearly: add Hatchet --pages 195 says what 195 is. In cmd_list, the f"{...:<{width}}" format pads every title to the longest one, which lines up the columns. stats has no arguments, so its subparser needs no add_argument lines at all.

#Step 5: main() ties it together

Every main() call is a separate "run": it loads books.json, does one thing, and saves. That's why the books from the first two calls are still there for list. The two failing calls return 1, and they save nothing, because the return 1 happens before save_books. That ordering matters: a command that failed halfway should never write a half-changed shelf to disk. Their error messages went to the error stream; in the terminal they look like the last line of the session at the top of this page.

path is a parameter with a default, so a test can call main(["stats"], path="test_books.json") and never touch your real reading history.

#Step 6: Split it into three files

Everything works, so now arrange it the way the diagram shows. Each file imports only what it uses, and books.py imports nothing at all, which is a good sign that the logic really is independent.

#The finished program

Mistakes on the command line itself never reach your code: argparse catches them and exits with code 2.

#Step 7: Write the README

Check your understanding

3 questions

1load_books returns [] for a missing file but raises an error for a damaged one. Why not return [] for both?

  • It opens fine; json.load is what fails.

  • A missing file is a normal first run; a damaged one holds data worth protecting.

  • It's caught right there in the except clause.

Show answer

B. A missing file is a normal first run; a damaged one holds data worth protecting.

2Why does main() call save_books only after the handler succeeds?

  • The return 1 in the except block skips the save.

  • Speed isn't the reason; protecting the data is.

  • They save harmlessly; it's the failed commands that must not.

Show answer

A. The return 1 in the except block skips the save.

3Why doesn't the JSON store a "finished": true field?

  • It can: true and false.

  • Store facts and calculate everything else, so the data can't contradict itself.

  • One field per book is tiny.

Show answer

B. Store facts and calculate everything else, so the data can't contradict itself.

Key takeaways

  • Design the commands and the data before the code; the session you sketch becomes your test and your README.
  • Treat a missing data file as an empty start, and a damaged one as an error that must not be overwritten.
  • Logic functions enforce rules by raising ValueError with a message a user can act on.
  • Handlers return messages, and main() alone prints, saves, and picks the exit code.
  • Save only after a command succeeds.
  • A logic module that imports nothing is a sign the layers are really separate.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add remove TITLE and rename OLD NEW commands.
  • Add --author to add, then have stats show your most-read author with collections.Counter.
  • Store the date each book was finished (as YYYY-MM-DD) and add stats --year 2026.
  • Add --file PATH to the main parser so you can keep separate shelves.

#Further reading

  • argparse: Sub-commands (opens in a new tab): every option add_subparsers and add_parser accept.
  • json: JSON encoder and decoder (opens in a new tab): load, dump, indent, and JSONDecodeError.
  • Command Line Interface Guidelines: Errors (opens in a new tab): how good tools phrase error messages so people can fix the problem themselves.

m7-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write the commands and data shape for a new tool before coding it.
  • Move printing and input out of logic functions so they can be tested.
  • Add subcommands and options, including choices and nargs.
  • Test a whole program by calling main() with lists and checking exit codes.
  • Protect stored data against missing, damaged, and wrong-shaped files.

These exercises use the patterns from the reading log: commands first, three layers, handlers that return messages, and main(argv=None) returning an exit code. Several solutions build on code from the build-along, so keep shelf.py, books.py, and storage.py open in another tab.

#Warm-up: which layer?

Sort these into interface, logic, or storage: (a) format_table(books), (b) load_books(path), (c) log_pages(books, title, pages), (d) build_parser(), (e) a function that decides whether a habit's streak is broken, (f) a function that writes a backup copy of books.json.

Answers: (a) interface, since it decides how things look. (b) and (f) storage. (c) and (e) logic, since they're rules about the data. (d) interface. If you hesitated on (e), ask: does it print, prompt, or touch a file? No, so it's logic.

#Exercise 1: Commands before code

A friend wants money.py to track pocket money: record money coming in and going out with a category (snacks, games, savings...), show the current balance, and list recent entries, optionally just one category. Write four example commands with the output each should print, and the JSON shape for the data file. No Python yet.

Need a hint?

Decide how a user types an amount going out. A separate spend command is clearer than asking people to type negative numbers. Then ask what each entry must remember for list to work.

Show solution

One good design (yours can differ, as long as every command's output can be produced from the stored data):

The balance isn't stored; it's the sum of the amounts, so it can never disagree with the entries. Storing spending as negative numbers internally keeps that sum simple, even though users never type a minus sign.

#Exercise 2: Untangle the report

This function reads scores, does the math, and prints, all at once. Split it into read_scores() (interface), summarize(scores) (logic, returns a dictionary), and format_summary(summary) (interface, returns a string). Make summarize([]) return sensible values instead of crashing, and test it with assert.

Need a hint?

summarize should return something like {"count": 3, "average": 72.3, "passing": 2}. For an empty list, None is an honest average. Write the asserts before you write summarize.

Show solution

The two asserts test the logic with no typing at all, including the boundary at exactly 60. The last line reads like a sentence: read, summarize, format, print. read_scores still crashes on abc; swapping in the validated loop from Module 5 is a one-function change now that input lives in one place.

#Exercise 3: Add remove and a sort option

Start from the planner parser in the notes. Add a remove ID subcommand (an integer), and give list a --sort option that only accepts due or title, defaulting to due. Check it by parsing ["remove", "3"], ["list"], and ["list", "--sort", "title", "--all"].

Need a hint?

add_argument("--sort", choices=["due", "title"], default="due") makes argparse reject anything else for you.

Show solution

--sort size would now fail with a usage message listing the allowed choices, and the help screen shows them too. Options can come in any order after the subcommand, which is why --all after --sort title works.

#Exercise 4: Test the whole program through main()

Here's a small calc.py. Write a helper exit_code(argv) that calls main(argv) and returns its exit code, including when argparse stops the program. Then assert these four results: total 2 3.5 gives 0, avg 70 --drop-lowest gives 1, mean 1 gives 2, and total two gives 2.

Need a hint?

When argparse rejects the command line it raises SystemExit, and the exception's .code attribute holds the exit code. Catch it with except SystemExit as stop:.

Show solution

total 2 3.5 also printed 5.5, which shows these are real runs of the program. The exit codes split mistakes into two kinds: 2 means "you typed the command wrong" (caught by argparse), and 1 means "the command made sense but couldn't be done" (caught by your own rules). nargs="+" collects one or more values into a list, which is how avg accepts any number of scores.

#Exercise 5: A loader that trusts nothing

load_books handles a missing file and broken JSON. But someone could hand-edit books.json into valid JSON of the wrong shape, like {"title": "Dune"}, a dictionary instead of a list, and every command would then crash in a confusing way. Write load_list(path) that returns [] for a missing file and raises a ValueError with a clear message for broken JSON or for anything that isn't a list. Test it on four files.

Need a hint?

After json.load, check isinstance(data, list). type(data).__name__ gives a readable name like dict for the message.

Show solution

A program's data file is input too, just like what people type, and it deserves the same suspicion. Checking the shape at the door means every other function can assume it really has a list.

#Exercise 6: Write the README for calc.py

Write a complete README for the calc.py tool from Exercise 4, covering the five questions: what it is, what you need, how to use it (with copyable examples of both commands and the option), how it's organized, and its limits.

Need a hint?

Run python calc.py -h and python calc.py avg -h and use the help text as a checklist: every command and option there should appear in an example.

Show solution

The "Exit codes" section isn't required for every tool, but it's what lets another program or a teacher's grading script use yours reliably. The example outputs let a reader check that their copy works.

#Challenge: Export the reading log to CSV

Add an export command to shelf.py that writes every book to a CSV file a spreadsheet can open, with the columns title, pages, read, and percent. It takes --output PATH (default books.csv) and refuses to overwrite an existing file unless --force is given. Put the file-writing in a function export_csv(books, path, force=False) that returns how many books it wrote, and test it before wiring it to the parser.

Need a hint?

csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=[...]) writes dictionaries as rows; call writeheader() first. Open the file with newline="", which the csv docs require so Windows doesn't get blank lines between rows. os.path.exists(path) tells you if the file is already there.

Show solution

{**book, "percent": percent} copies the book's fields and adds one more, without changing the stored book. Then wire it in: export_csv goes in storage.py, and shelf.py gets a handler and a subparser.

Because export_csv raises ValueError, the existing main() already turns "file exists" into an error: line and exit code 1. No change to main() at all: that's the payoff of the design.
