What you'll learn

  • Choose a capstone project that fits your time and skills.
  • Write a one-page plan: commands, sample output, data shape, and functions in each layer.
  • Define the trickiest rule in your project in plain words, with examples, before coding it.
  • Break the build into milestones that each end with something you can run.

Close VS Code tonight. Tomorrow morning, open a terminal and type python habits.py list. If it prints read 20 pages streak 12, your program remembered something across a night, a restart, and maybe a laptop update. That's the whole capstone in one sentence: build a command-line tool that people would actually use every day, and that never loses or garbles their data.

You'll use everything from Modules 2 through 7: collections to model the data, functions with clear inputs and outputs, JSON files, validation, debugging, and the three-layer design. This lesson is about planning. The next one builds a complete example in milestones, and the last one covers testing, polish, and presenting.

#What every project must include

Requirement What counts You learned it in
Persistence data saved to JSON and loaded on the next run; a missing file is a fresh start; a damaged file is reported, never overwritten Module 4
At least 4 subcommands including one that changes saved data and one that searches or filters it Module 7
Validation every value from the command line is checked, with a message that says how to fix it Module 5
Collections at least two used for a reason (dict for lookup by name, set for "seen it?", Counter for totals...) Module 2
Dates or randomness datetime for anything about days, or random for anything shuffled Module 5
Clear errors no tracebacks for user mistakes; exit code 0 on success and nonzero on failure Modules 5 and 7
Layers interface, logic, and storage in separate modules; logic never prints Module 7
Tests at least 8 unittest tests, including edge cases Lessons 2 and 3 of this module
README the five questions: what, setup, usage, files, limits Module 7

#Pick a project

All five ideas meet the requirements. The difference is how much logic sits in the middle.

Project Level Core commands The interesting part
To-do list with due dates starter add, list, done, remove, list --overdue sorting by due date, and "overdue" depends on today
Habit tracker (built in the next lesson) core add, check, list, history, remove streaks: counting days in a row, across months
Flash-card trainer core add, quiz, search, stats spaced repetition: cards you miss come back sooner (a Leitner box system)
Expense tracker with budgets stretch spend, earn, list, budget, report monthly totals per category with defaultdict, and warnings near a budget
Club gear checkout stretch add, checkout, return, overdue, search who has what, due dates, and refusing to lend an item twice

Pick the one you would use. If none fits, invent one with the same shape: a list of records, a few commands that change them, and at least one rule that's harder than adding and removing. A practice log for an instrument, a reading-challenge tracker, or a chore rotation that assigns jobs fairly would all work.

💡 Tip

If you've never built a multi-file program before, start with the to-do list and add features from a harder project once the requirements pass. A finished starter project beats an abandoned stretch one.

#The one-page plan

Copy this into a file called PLAN.md in your project folder and fill it in before writing any Python. Expect to change it as you build; that's what it's for.

#A worked plan: the habit tracker

Here's the plan for the project you'll see built in the next lesson, filled in the way yours should be.

Commands and output. Sketched first, exactly as a user would see them:

Data shape.

Every choice in that file has a reason, and writing the reasons down is part of the plan:

  • A dictionary keyed by name, because every command finds a habit by name, and a dict lookup beats searching a list. Names are stored lowercase, so Read and read are the same habit.
  • Dates as YYYY-MM-DD strings, because JSON has no date type, and this format sorts correctly as plain text.
  • A list of days in the file, a set in memory. JSON has no sets either. But "was this day done?" is the question the streak code asks over and over, and day in some_set answers it instantly.
  • No stored streaks. A streak can be calculated from the days, so storing it would only create a second copy that could disagree with the first.
  • An outer {"habits": ...} wrapper, so a future version can add settings next to it without breaking old files.

Functions by layer. Interface: build_parser, one cmd_ handler per command, main(argv, path, today). Logic: normalize, add_habit, check_in, current_streak, longest_streak, history_strip. Storage: load_data, save_data.

Notice that today is a parameter. The logic never calls date.today() itself. That's how the tests in Lesson 3 can pretend it's November 15 forever.

#Find the hard part early

Every project has one rule that's harder than the rest. For the habit tracker, it's the streak. Before writing any code, pin it down in words and with examples, because most capstone bugs are really vague definitions.

The current streak is the number of days in a row, ending today, on which the habit was done. If today isn't checked in yet, count back from yesterday instead, so the streak doesn't drop to 0 every morning.

Days done (November) Today Current streak Why
13, 14, 15 15 3 three in a row ending today
13, 14 15 2 today not done yet, so count from the 14th
10, 11, 13 15 0 the 14th was missed
Oct 31, Nov 1 Nov 1 2 the streak crosses a month boundary

That table is already four test cases. Write the same kind of table for your hardest rule: when a flash card moves boxes, when an expense counts toward this month, when a checkout becomes overdue.

#Milestones that each end with something running

Milestone Done when...
M1 Storage load and save round-trip your example data, and a missing file gives an empty start
M2 First command add works and refuses duplicates and blank names
M3 The main change the command that updates records works, with its validation
M4 The hard rule the table from "Find the hard part early" passes as asserts
M5 Full command line every command runs through main(), with errors and exit codes
M6 Tests and README 8 or more unittest tests pass, and a stranger could use the tool from the README

Run your program at the end of every milestone, and keep a copy that works before starting the next one. Committing it with git, if you use it, or zipping the folder both count.

Must have is the requirements table. Nice to have is everything else: colors, a --json output mode, CSV export, an undo command. Write nice-to-haves down so you stop thinking about them, then ignore them until the must-haves pass.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The habit file stores days as a list of "YYYY-MM-DD" strings. Why not store date objects or a set?

  • Space isn't the issue here.

  • The program converts back to a set of dates after loading, when it needs fast lookups.

  • They can; the problem is only saving them as JSON.

Show answer

B. The program converts back to a set of dates after loading, when it needs fast lookups.

2Why do the logic functions take today as a parameter instead of calling date.today()?

  • A test that depends on the real date passes today and fails tomorrow.

  • It's fast; the reason is control, not speed.

  • They can import it; they just shouldn't decide what day it is.

Show answer

A. A test that depends on the real date passes today and fails tomorrow.

3Your plan has eight nice-to-have features and two must-haves still failing. What's the best next step?

  • Unfinished requirements are what the rubric checks.

  • Writing them down lets you stop thinking about them without losing the ideas.

  • The plan is fine; the order of work is the issue.

Show answer

B. Writing them down lets you stop thinking about them without losing the ideas.

Key takeaways

  • Plan on one page: commands and output, data shape, functions by layer, the hard rule, bad inputs, milestones.
  • Choose the data shape for the questions your commands ask: dicts for lookup by name, sets for "did this happen?"
  • Store facts, not things you can calculate.
  • Pass today into logic so the date is something tests can control.
  • Define the hardest rule with a table of examples; those rows become your first tests.
  • Every milestone ends with a program that runs.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Start from a starter skeleton and fill it in one milestone at a time, running something at each step.
  • Save JSON safely by writing a temporary file and swapping it in.
  • Store dates as text and calculate with them as date objects and timedeltas.
  • Turn a rule written in plain words (the streak) into code, and check it against a table of examples.
  • Connect everything through main(argv, path, today) so the whole tool can be tested.

This is the habit tracker from the plan in Lesson 1, built for real. If you chose a different project, build along anyway with your own project open beside it: each milestone here matches one of yours, and the decisions (what to validate, where today comes from, when to save) carry straight over.

#The starter

Make a folder called habits with three empty files: storage.py, tracker.py (the logic), and habits.py (the command line). Here are the signatures to aim for. Each milestone below fills some of them in.

raise NotImplementedError is a placeholder that crashes loudly if you call a function you haven't written yet, which is much better than a silent pass that returns None.

#Milestone 1: Storage you can trust

The new idea is in save_data. Opening a file with "w" empties it immediately, so if the program crashed (or the laptop died) halfway through json.dump, the real file would be left half-written and the user's history gone. Writing to habits.json.tmp first and then calling os.replace avoids that: the swap happens in one step, so habits.json is always either the old complete file or the new complete one. The shape check in load_data catches a file that's valid JSON but not our JSON.

Checkpoint: the round trip asserts pass, a missing file prints the empty tracker, and a damaged file produces an error: line, not a traceback.

#Milestone 2: Add habits, and decide what a name is

" ".join(name.split()) is a small trick worth remembering: split() with no argument breaks on any run of whitespace and drops the ends, and join puts single spaces back. Every function that takes a name goes through normalize, so Read 20 Pages, read 20 pages, and READ 20 pages all find the same habit. get_habit exists because three commands need "find this habit or explain why not," and writing that once means the message is the same everywhere.

Checkpoint: duplicates, blank names, and very long names are rejected with readable messages.

#Milestone 3: Check-ins, with dates stored as text

Dates live in two forms. In the file they're "2026-11-14" strings, because JSON can't hold anything else. In the logic they're date objects, because those can be compared (day > today) and stepped (today - timedelta(days=1)). isoformat() and fromisoformat() convert between the two, and done_days builds a set, because the streak code is about to ask "is this day in there?" many times. Sorting after each append keeps the file readable when someone checks in for a past day.

Checkpoint: repeat check-ins and future dates are rejected; a check-in for any past day works.

#Milestone 4: The streak, from words to code

The plan defined it in words: days in a row ending today; if today isn't done yet, count back from yesterday instead. The code is that sentence, almost word for word. Step through it with today not yet checked in, and watch day walk backward until it hits a gap:

Now the full set of streak functions, checked against the table from the plan:

longest_streak only starts counting at days that begin a run (the day before isn't in the set), then counts forward. That way each run is measured once, instead of re-counting from every day inside it. The month-boundary row passes without any special code: timedelta knows October has 31 days, which is the reason to use it instead of subtracting 1 from a day number.

Checkpoint: every row of the streak table passes as an assert.

#Milestone 5: The command line

Every handler takes (data, args, today) and returns a message. main is the same shape as the reading log's, plus one new parameter: today, which defaults to the real date but can be fixed for testing.

Each main() call loads habits.json, runs one command, and saves, exactly like separate runs in the terminal. The two failures at the end return 1, their messages go to the error stream, and nothing is saved for them. --date uses the iso_date type from Module 5's practice, so --date 11/14 is rejected by argparse before any of your code runs, while --days 3 is a perfectly good integer that cmd_history rejects with its own range rule.

Checkpoint: every command runs through main(), and every mistake ends with an error: line and exit code 1 or 2.

#Split it into three files

Move each piece into the file the plan gave it: the Milestone 1 functions into storage.py, Milestones 2 to 4 into tracker.py, and Milestone 5 into habits.py. The top of habits.py imports from the other two, and the bottom gets the usual guard:

tracker.py needs from datetime import date, timedelta at its top, and storage.py needs import json and import os. The parentheses around the long from tracker import (...) line let it continue onto a second line. Then run it for real in the VS Code terminal. On November 15, 2026, a session looks like this:

Close the terminal, open a new one, and run python habits.py list again. The streak is still there. That's the capstone's main requirement, working.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does save_data write habits.json.tmp and then call os.replace, instead of writing habits.json directly?

  • It can; "w" mode empties the file first, which is exactly the risk.

  • Until the swap, the old complete file is still in place; after it, the new complete one is.

  • The temporary file is replaced into the real one, so no backup is kept.

Show answer

B. Until the swap, the old complete file is still in place; after it, the new complete one is.

2The streak counts back from yesterday when today isn't checked in. What would happen without that rule?

  • The rule is about what "current streak" should mean to a person, written down in the plan before the code.

  • Nothing crashes; the number would just be misleading.

  • timedelta handles month boundaries either way.

Show answer

A. The rule is about what "current streak" should mean to a person, written down in the plan before the code.

3cmd_history checks 7 <= args.days <= 60 itself. Why not let argparse do all the checking?

  • type=int checks that it is an integer; the allowed range is a rule of this program.

  • Raising ValueError makes the range message look like every other error and return exit code 1.

  • Optional arguments can have types and choices like any other.

Show answer

B. Raising ValueError makes the range message look like every other error and return exit code 1.

Key takeaways

  • Run something at the end of every milestone; never write three milestones before testing one.
  • Write JSON to a temporary file and os.replace it, so a crash can't destroy the data.
  • Keep dates as YYYY-MM-DD text in the file and as date objects in the logic; convert at the boundary.
  • A rule defined in words, with a table of examples, turns almost line for line into code and asserts.
  • Passing today into main() and the logic is what makes the whole program testable, which is the next lesson.

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write a test plan that covers normal use, edge cases, and bad input.
  • Write unittest tests with assertEqual, assertRaises, setUp, and tearDown.
  • Test storage safely with a temporary folder, and test whole commands through main().
  • Run tests from the terminal and from the VS Code Testing view.
  • Polish, present, and assess your project with the rubric.

Your tool works when you use it, because you know which commands exist and you type dates the right way. Then a friend tries it and, within a minute, types python habits.py check Read --date tomorrow. Testing is how you find out what happens next before they do. This lesson uses the habit tracker from Lesson 2, and every technique applies to your project.

#Start with a test plan

List what to test before writing any test code. Three kinds of cases catch most bugs: normal use, edge cases at the boundaries, and bad input.

Area Normal Edge Bad input
Streaks three days in a row ending today today not checked yet; crossing a month; no days at all (not user input)
Habits add a new name same name with different capitals or spaces blank name; 31 characters; duplicate
Check-ins check in today a past date future date; same day twice; unknown habit; --date 11/14
Storage save then load gives the same data no file yet damaged JSON; valid JSON of the wrong shape
Commands data survives between runs list with no habits missing subcommand; unknown subcommand

Every row in your Lesson 1 table for the hardest rule belongs in here. So does every bug you've already fixed: that's the regression-check habit from Module 6.

#Your first unittest tests

assert statements stop at the first failure. The unittest module, built into Python, runs every test, reports each one by name, and tells you exactly what was expected. Here's the logic and storage code from Lesson 2, condensed into one cell so the tests below have something real to test:

A test is a method whose name starts with test_, inside a class that inherits from unittest.TestCase. Inside it, self.assertEqual(actual, expected) checks a result:

Name each test after the behavior it checks, as a sentence: test_streak_survives_until_today_is_checked tells you what broke without opening the file. The little run() helper exists only for this page; in your project you'll run tests from the terminal, shown further down.

#Watch a test catch a bug

Tests earn their keep when someone "improves" the code later. Suppose you decide the grace rule is unnecessary and simplify current_streak to always count from today:

One test fails, by name, with the exact numbers: it expected 2 and got 0. Without the test, you'd find out when a user's 40-day streak showed 0 one morning. The last line puts the working version back for the tests below.

#Test errors and files without touching real data

assertRaises checks that bad input is refused. Used with with, the test passes only if the code inside raises that exception. For storage, setUp runs before every test and tearDown after it; here they create and delete a temporary folder, so tests never read or overwrite your real habits.json.

setUp gives each test a fresh tracker with one habit. Tests must not depend on each other: if test_double_check_in_is_rejected left a check-in behind for the next test, the order tests run in could change the results.

#Test whole commands through main()

Unit tests check pieces. A few end-to-end tests check that the pieces are wired together: call main() with a list of words, a temporary path, and a fixed today, and capture what it prints. In your project they go in test_habits.py next to the other tests, which import from your three modules:

redirect_stdout and redirect_stderr catch the printed output in memory, so the test can check the message and the terminal stays clean. The first test is the capstone's main promise, written as code: data saved by one run is there for the next. With all four test classes in the file, run them from the project folder:

python -m unittest finds every file in the folder whose name starts with test and runs every test in it. In VS Code you can also run Python: Configure Tests from the Command Palette, choose unittest, then accept the folder and file pattern it suggests; the beaker icon in the Activity Bar then opens the Test Explorer, with a green run button next to each test in the editor's margin. Right-click that button and choose Debug Test to step through a failing test with the debugger from Module 6.

#Polish: the last 10% people notice first

Work through this list with fresh eyes, ideally the day after you finish the code.

  • Every message helps. Each error: line says what went wrong and what to do. Read them all by triggering each one.
  • Help text is complete. Run -h on the tool and on every subcommand. Every argument has a help= string, and defaults are mentioned.
  • No leftovers. No debug prints, no commented-out code blocks, no unused imports, no NotImplementedError stubs.
  • Names tell the truth. A function called get_habit doesn't also change data.
  • The README is current. Every example in it runs, exactly as written, on a fresh folder.
  • The hallway test. Give the tool and README to someone who hasn't seen it. Don't explain anything. Watch what they type first, and fix whatever confused them.

Here's the README for the finished habit tracker:

#Present it in three minutes

A short demo shows what you built and how you think. Use this outline, and rehearse it once with a timer.

  1. The problem (20 seconds). Who is it for, and what did they do before it existed?
  2. Live demo (90 seconds). Run three or four commands that tell a story: add, use it a few times, show the result. Start from an empty data file so the audience sees it build up. Have the commands ready in a text file to paste.
  3. Break it on purpose (30 seconds). Type something wrong and show the helpful error. Then close the terminal, reopen it, and run list to show nothing was lost.
  4. One thing you learned (30 seconds). A bug you chased and the test that now guards it, or a design decision you'd make differently.
  5. Next steps (10 seconds). One feature you'd add with another week.

#Rubric

Score each row from 1 to 4. A 3 in every row is a strong, complete project.

Criterion 4: Excellent 3: Solid 2: Developing 1: Beginning
Persistence data survives restarts; missing and damaged files handled; saves are crash-safe data survives restarts; missing file handled saves work, but a missing or damaged file crashes the tool data is lost between runs
Commands 5 or more subcommands, including update and search, all with help text 4 subcommands, including update and search 3 subcommands, or update or search is missing 1 or 2 commands, or input via prompts only
Validation and errors every bad input gets a clear, actionable message and the right exit code bad input never shows a traceback some bad input crashes with a traceback no validation
Design three modules; logic never prints or reads files; today and paths are parameters three layers, with small slips logic and printing mixed in places one long script
Data and collections data shape chosen for the commands, with reasons written down; 2 or more collections used well sensible data shape; 2 collections used works, but awkward shape or calculated values stored data shape fights the program
Tests 12 or more tests covering normal, edge, bad input, and whole commands; all pass 8 or more passing tests, including edge cases a few tests, or some failing no tests
README and presentation a stranger can install and use it from the README alone; demo is clear and timed README covers the five questions; demo works README missing setup or examples no README

#Reflect, then keep going

Write a short paragraph answering these, and keep it with your project: Which bug took longest to find, and what evidence finally cracked it? Which design decision from your plan held up, and which did you change? If you started over tomorrow, what would you do first?

When you're ready for more, each of these builds directly on what you made:

  • Better tests: pytest (opens in a new tab) runs your unittest tests unchanged and makes new ones shorter.
  • A real database: the built-in sqlite3 (opens in a new tab) module stores records in one file and lets you query them, a natural step up from JSON once you have thousands of records.
  • A nicer terminal: third-party packages like Rich add colors and tables; list them in requirements.txt the way Module 5 showed.
  • A different interface: keep tracker.py and storage.py exactly as they are and write a new interface layer, such as a window with the built-in tkinter module. If your layers are truly separate, the logic won't need a single change, which is the best test of your design there is.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Why do the storage tests use tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() instead of the real habits.json?

  • Speed isn't the reason.

  • setUp makes a fresh folder and tearDown deletes it, every time.

  • It can; using your real data would make tests unsafe and unpredictable.

Show answer

B. setUp makes a fresh folder and tearDown deletes it, every time.

2After a refactor, one test fails: AssertionError: 0 != 2 in test_streak_survives_until_today_is_checked. What's the best next step?

  • That deletes the requirement instead of keeping it.

  • The test names the rule that broke and shows the expected and actual values.

  • Then the bug ships, and nothing will catch it next time.

Show answer

B. The test names the rule that broke and shows the expected and actual values.

Key takeaways

  • Plan tests in three kinds: normal, edge, and bad input; every past bug becomes a test.
  • A unittest test is a test_ method in a TestCase class; name it as a sentence about behavior.
  • assertRaises proves bad input is refused; setUp/tearDown give every test a clean start.
  • Test files in a temporary folder and pass a fixed today, so tests never touch real data or depend on the calendar.
  • End-to-end tests call main() with a list of words and check the exit code and output.
  • Polish with fresh eyes and a hallway test, then demo the story: problem, use, failure handled, lesson learned.
